title: What is Code?
description: Code is instructions for computers. But really, it's a way to express ideas. Let's start there.

learningObjectives.text: Define what code is in plain language
Explain why the current moment (Claude era) is special for learning to code
Describe what lazy coding means and why it's smart

contentSections.body: Every app on your phone — Instagram, Google Maps, your banking app — was written in code by humans who also occasionally forgot what they were doing and Googled 'how to center a div'. Code isn't magic. It's instructions.

**Code** is a set of instructions you write for a computer. Think of it like a recipe:

- A recipe tells a cook: "First add flour, then mix in eggs, then bake at 180°C."
- Code tells a computer: "First ask the user for their name, then store it, then display it on screen."

The computer follows your instructions exactly. Which is both its superpower and its greatest limitation.

contentSections.question: Before we go further — who do you think code is actually written for: computers or humans?
contentSections.answer: **Humans.** Computers could run binary (1s and 0s) all day. Code exists so that *humans* can read, write, and reason about what a program does. A computer doesn't care if your variable is named `x` or `userEmailAddress` — but the next person reading your code will care a lot.
contentSections.hint: Think about who needs to understand what the code does day-to-day.

contentSections.body: Code = instructions written by humans, for humans, that computers can also execute.

### Era 1: Manual (1950s–1990s)
You write everything from scratch. No Google. No libraries. You understand every line because you wrote every line. It takes forever.

### Era 2: Stack Overflow (1995–2022)
You Google your problem, find an answer, copy-paste, and tweak until it works. You might not fully understand why — but it ships. 90% of professional coding in this era.

### Era 3: Claude (2023–now)
You describe what you want in plain language. Claude writes the code. You review, tweak, and ship. **You learn faster** because Claude explains as it goes.

**You're learning to code at the best possible time.** The tools available to you right now — Claude, VS Code, Vercel — make it possible to ship real things in days, not months. Don't let anyone tell you "you should have started 5 years ago."

"Lazy coding" isn't about being sloppy. It's about being **efficient with your most limited resource: your energy**.

Traditional coding education says: *Learn theory first. Build from scratch. Suffer through the fundamentals.*

Lazy coding says:
1. **Use the best tools available.** Claude is insanely good at boilerplate. Let it write the boring parts.
2. **Ship something real.** You learn more from deploying one real app than reading 10 tutorials.
3. **Understand enough to steer.** You don't need to memorize syntax. You need to understand what's happening so you can spot bugs and ask better questions.

**This course is built for people who code from bed.** If you have a chronic illness, limited energy, or just prefer working in pajamas — this curriculum respects that. Each lesson is designed to be completable in 15 minutes. Each pod is 5 minutes. Do one pod at a time if that's all you have.
Lazy coding = using Claude for the tedious parts, understanding enough to guide it, and shipping things that work.

title: Why Claude?
description: What Claude can do. How it differs from Google. When to trust it, when to push back.

learningObjectives.text: Explain at a high level how Claude generates code
List Claude's top strengths for coding tasks
Identify when Claude's output should be verified or questioned

contentSections.body: Imagine a developer who has read every Stack Overflow answer, every GitHub repository, every technical blog post ever written — and can synthesize it all into code *for your specific situation*, in seconds. That's roughly what Claude is.

Claude is a **large language model (LLM)** — an AI trained on billions of examples of human writing, including enormous amounts of code, documentation, and technical discussion.

When you ask Claude to write a React component, it's not looking it up or running a search. It's generating the most statistically likely good answer based on patterns it learned during training.

This is different from:
- **Google**: Returns pages that mention your query. You still have to read and adapt.
- **Stack Overflow**: Returns solutions to *similar* problems. You adapt to your context.
- **Claude**: Generates a solution *for your exact context* in one step.

contentSections.question: If Claude learned from code written before its training cutoff, what happens when you ask it about a very new library released last month?
contentSections.answer: **Claude might confidently give you wrong information.** It may not know the new library exists, or it may hallucinate plausible-sounding but incorrect APIs. Always check docs for libraries released after Claude's training cutoff (April 2024). Ask Claude: *"What version of [library] are you familiar with?"*
contentSections.hint: Think about the gap between when Claude learned things and when you're asking.

contentSections.title: What Claude is great at (and what it's not)

contentSections.body:
### Claude's superpowers for coding:

**Boilerplate generation** — Authentication forms, API routes, database queries, CRUD operations. Claude has seen thousands of examples. It gets these right fast.

**Explaining code** — Paste in mysterious code and ask "what does this do?" Claude is excellent at this.

**Refactoring** — "Make this cleaner" or "make this more performant" gets real results.

**Debugging** — Paste an error + the relevant code. Claude usually spots the issue immediately.

**Brainstorming** — "What's the best way to structure a habit tracker app?" Good starting points.

contentSections.scenario: You're about to lean on Claude for a big coding task. Before you do, it's worth knowing where it can quietly let you down.
contentSections.question: Select every real limitation Claude has as a coding partner.

items.label: It struggles with truly novel, cutting-edge problems it's never seen before
It can confidently describe APIs or functions that don't actually exist
It loses track of context once a codebase gets very large (~100K+ tokens)
It doesn't know about real-time data — today's prices, news, or events
It's generally bad at generating boilerplate like auth forms or CRUD routes
It will always sneak in extra libraries you didn't ask for

explanation.novel: True — if your problem is genuinely unique (new algorithm, cutting-edge research), Claude has less to work from.
explanation.hallucination: True — this is hallucination. Claude can confidently describe APIs, functions, or libraries that don't exist. Always test the code.
explanation.context: True — Claude loses context after roughly 100K tokens. It can't hold your entire app in mind.
explanation.realtime: True — Claude doesn't know what happened yesterday. Prices, news, live data aren't available to it.
explanation.boilerplate: Actually the opposite — boilerplate (auth forms, API routes, CRUD operations) is one of Claude's strengths. It's seen thousands of examples and gets these right fast.
explanation.extra-libs: Not something you learned as a stated limitation — Claude doesn't have a fixed habit of sneaking in libraries. Still always worth checking imports against your constraints, just not one of its core weaknesses.

contentSections.synthesis: The pattern: Claude is strong on well-trodden ground (boilerplate, explaining, refactoring, debugging common issues) and weaker at the edges — genuinely novel problems, anything after its training cutoff, and anything requiring it to hold a huge codebase in mind at once. Knowing which kind of task you're handing it tells you how much to double-check.

contentSections.body: **Always run Claude's code before trusting it.** A hallucinated function name won't throw an error until runtime. The fastest way to catch Claude mistakes: paste the code into your editor and run it.

The best mental model for working with Claude: **a brilliant but overconfident intern**.

- Fast and eager
- Knows a lot of patterns
- Occasionally makes confident mistakes
- Gets better when you give more context
- Needs your review before shipping

Your job isn't to write all the code. Your job is to:
1. **Describe the goal clearly**
2. **Review what Claude produces**
3. **Spot problems** (wrong logic, outdated APIs, security issues)
4. **Ask follow-up questions** ("Why did you do it this way? What are the tradeoffs?")
Claude is a brilliant, fast, occasionally overconfident coding partner. You steer; it drafts. You verify; it generates.

title: Anatomy of a Good Prompt
description: How to ask Claude for code. The four-part structure that consistently gets great results.

learningObjectives.text: Identify the four components of an effective coding prompt
Distinguish a good prompt from a bad one
Write a well-structured prompt that produces useful code

contentSections.body: Marcus types: *"write a login form"*. Claude produces something. It works, kind of. But it's not React, it's not his tech stack, and the error handling is wrong. He spends 40 minutes adapting it. Sound familiar?

contentSections.question: What's missing from this prompt: "Write a login form"?
contentSections.answer:
Almost everything Claude needs to give you something useful:
- **What framework?** React? Plain HTML? Vue?
- **What styling?** Tailwind? CSS modules? No styling?
- **What should it do?** Just collect input? Call an API? Handle errors?
- **What format?** Full component? Just the JSX? With TypeScript?

Without this, Claude guesses — and its guess might not match your project.
contentSections.hint: Think about what decisions Claude has to make when you give it no constraints.

contentSections.body:
A good prompt has **four parts**:

1. **Context** — What's the situation? What project are you building?
2. **Task** — What exactly should the code do?
3. **Constraints** — Which tech, libraries, or requirements apply?
4. **Output format** — Code only? Code + explanation? With comments?

contentSections.intro: Time to build Marcus's prompt for real — the one that gets a login form matching his actual project, not a generic guess.

fields.question: What should open the prompt — the very first thing Claude needs to know?

options.label: State the tech stack
options.value: I'm building a React app with TypeScript that uses Tailwind CSS.

options.label: Jump straight to the ask

fields.correctValue: I'm building a React app with TypeScript that uses Tailwind CSS.

feedback.I'm building a React app with TypeScript: Right — this tells Claude what to target before anything else. Skip it and Claude has to guess your framework and styling.
feedback.Write a login form: This is the bad-prompt version — no context means Claude guesses your framework, your styling, everything.

fields.question: What should the task section actually specify?

options.label: The concrete requirements
options.value:
I need a login form component that:
- Takes email + password inputs
- Validates email format before submit
- Shows a loading spinner while submitting
- Displays error messages inline (not in an alert)
- Calls a /api/login endpoint on submit

options.label: Just say it should be good

fields.correctValue:
I need a login form component that:
- Takes email + password inputs
- Validates email format before submit
- Shows a loading spinner while submitting
- Displays error messages inline (not in an alert)
- Calls a /api/login endpoint on submit

feedback.I need a login form component that:\n- T: Right — each bullet is a concrete, checkable requirement. Claude can't get these wrong by guessing.
feedback.Make it good and modern: "Good" and "modern" mean nothing specific to Claude. It'll invent its own definition, which may not match what you need.

fields.question: What should you tell Claude about the output format?

options.label: Component + types + comments + assumptions
options.value:
Please provide:
- The React component with TypeScript types
- Brief comments explaining each section
- Any assumptions you made

options.label: Don't specify — let it decide

fields.correctValue:
Please provide:
- The React component with TypeScript types
- Brief comments explaining each section
- Any assumptions you made

feedback.Please provide:\n- The React component w: Right — and asking for "assumptions you made" specifically is what surfaces hidden problems before they bite you.
feedback.(nothing specified): Leaving this open means you might get a wall of prose, untyped JS, or no explanation of tradeoffs — you won't know until you've already spent time reading it.

contentSections.synthesis: This is the lesson's own good-prompt example, built field by field: Context tells Claude what you're building, Task spells out the concrete requirements, and Output format tells it exactly what to hand back — including its own assumptions, so you can catch mistakes fast. Sixty extra seconds writing this saves the forty minutes Marcus spent adapting a generic guess.

contentSections.body: **Pro move:** After Claude responds, always ask: *"What assumptions did you make? What are the tradeoffs of this approach?"* This surfaces hidden issues before they bite you.

You don't have to get the prompt perfect the first time. Good prompting is a **conversation**:

1. Start with the four-part prompt
2. Claude produces something
3. Identify what's wrong or incomplete
4. Follow up: *"This is good, but I need the error messages to appear below each field, not above. Also add a 'forgot password' link."*
5. Iterate until it's right

Each follow-up should be specific. Don't say "this doesn't work." Say "When I submit with a blank email field, the form submits anyway. Add validation that requires a valid email before allowing submit."

**Sarah's workflow:** She keeps a "prompt scratch pad" — a notes file where she drafts her prompts before sending them. She adds context, clarifies the task, lists constraints. Takes 2 minutes. Saves 30.
Structure every coding prompt: Context → Task → Constraints → Output format. Then iterate.

title: Write Your First Prompt
description: From theory to practice. You'll write a real prompt, get code back, and understand what happened.

learningObjectives.text: Write a complete four-part prompt for a specific use case
Identify the parts of Claude's response that need verification
Formulate a good follow-up prompt based on Claude's output

contentSections.body: Alex wants to build a simple tool for their team: a form that captures feature requests and emails them. No database. No authentication. Just: fill out a form, get an email. Let's write that prompt together.

Here's how Alex builds the prompt, piece by piece:

**Context:**
```
I'm building a simple web page for internal use at my company.
No framework — just HTML, CSS, and vanilla JavaScript.
```

**Task:**
```
I need a feature request form that:
- Takes: name, email, feature title, description (textarea)
- On submit, sends a POST request to /api/submit-feature
- Shows a success message after submit
- Clears the form after success
```

**Constraints:**
```
- No external libraries
- Works in modern browsers (Chrome, Firefox, Safari)
- Mobile-friendly layout
```

**Output format:**
```
Provide complete HTML/CSS/JS in one file. Add comments explaining the JavaScript.
```
**Notice:** The prompt doesn't try to explain everything at once. It describes the end result, not the implementation. Claude figures out the implementation.

contentSections.scenario: Claude just responded with the HTML/CSS/JS for Alex's feature-request form.
contentSections.question: Select every check you should actually run before running this code.

items.label: Did Claude sneak in a library you didn't ask for?
Do the function/endpoint names actually exist, or just sound plausible?
Is there a .catch() or try/catch, or does a failed request just go silent?
Does the logic actually do what you asked, or just look right at a glance?
Whether the code is under some fixed number of lines
Whether every variable name uses camelCase

explanation.constraints: Yes — e.g. importing Bootstrap when you said no external libraries. Claude can quietly drift from your stated constraints.
explanation.hallucinated-fns: Yes — hallucinated functions have plausible-sounding names. If you see fetch('/api/submit-feature', ...), confirm that endpoint is real.
explanation.error-handling: Yes — Claude often skips error handling unless you ask for it explicitly.
explanation.logic-matches: Yes — read through the code. Don't just run it; understand what it actually does versus what you intended.
explanation.line-count: Not a real signal — a short response can still be wrong, and a long one can still be correct. Length isn't a proxy for quality.
explanation.camel-case: A style preference, not a correctness check — it won't tell you if the code actually works or matches your constraints.

contentSections.synthesis: The real checklist is about behavior, not appearance: does it respect your constraints, are the names it invented actually real, does it handle failure, and does the logic match your intent. Skim for those four before you ever hit run.

contentSections.question: Claude's code does exactly what you asked, but it doesn't handle the case where the network request fails. What should you do?
contentSections.answer:
**Follow up with a specific request:** *"Add error handling for network failures. If the POST request fails, show an error message below the form and re-enable the submit button."*

Don't restart from scratch. Claude has context from your conversation. Build on what's already working.
contentSections.hint: You don't need to rewrite the whole prompt — just point out the specific gap.

contentSections.body:
**Mistake 1: Too vague**
*"Build me a website"* → Claude doesn't know where to start.

**Mistake 2: Too specific too early**
*"Write code that calls fetch with method POST, Content-Type application/json, and uses async/await"* → You're specifying the implementation, not the goal. Let Claude choose the implementation.

**Mistake 3: No context**
*"Add authentication"* → To what? In what stack? Which auth method?

**Mistake 4: Combining too many tasks**
*"Build the entire user dashboard including login, profile, settings, and notifications"* → Too much for one prompt. Break it into steps. Start with login, get it working, then add profile.

**One task at a time is faster.** It feels slower to write 4 prompts instead of 1, but each focused prompt gets a more accurate result. Four focused prompts → 4 working pieces. One mega-prompt → one messy, partially-working blob.
Start with context + task + constraints + output format. Read the response critically. Follow up on gaps. Build incrementally.

title: Set Up Your Workspace
description: VS Code, Node.js, and git. Three tools. That's all you need to start building.

learningObjectives.text: Identify the purpose of VS Code, Node.js, and git in a coding workflow
Describe the correct order of installation steps
Run your first terminal command to verify a successful setup

contentSections.body: You need exactly three things: a text editor (VS Code), a JavaScript runtime (Node.js), and a version control system (git). That's it. Everything else — frameworks, libraries, deployment tools — comes later.

contentSections.intro: Before the details — assemble the toolkit itself. Three slots, one tool each.

fields.prompt: Which text editor goes in your toolkit?

options.label: VS Code
Notepad

fields.correctValue: VS Code

feedback.VS Code: Right — free, fast, and used by ~75% of professional developers, with extensions for everything.
feedback.Notepad: Notepad works in a pinch, but it has none of the extensions, syntax highlighting, or git integration that make VS Code the standard choice.

fields.prompt: Which JavaScript runtime lets you run JS outside the browser?

options.label: Node.js
Python

fields.correctValue: Node.js

feedback.Node.js: Right — Node.js runs JavaScript on your computer, and its installer also gives you npm, the package manager for installing libraries.
feedback.Python: Python is a real language, but it doesn't run JavaScript — you need Node.js for that.

fields.prompt: Which tool tracks changes and lets you recover deleted files?

options.label: git
Dropbox

fields.correctValue: git

feedback.git: Right — every git commit is a save point. Delete a file by mistake, and you can recover it from the last commit.
feedback.Dropbox: Dropbox syncs files, but it doesn't give you commit history or the ability to recover one specific file from one specific point in time the way git does.

contentSections.synthesis: VS Code, Node.js, git — exactly the three tools this lesson opened with. Everything else (frameworks, libraries, deployment tools) comes later, once these three are in place.

contentSections.question: You delete a file by mistake and realize 3 hours later. Which tool helps you recover it?
contentSections.answer:
**git**, if you've committed the file before deleting it. This is why you commit often — every commit is a save point you can return to.

`git checkout HEAD -- filename.js` recovers the file from the last commit.
contentSections.hint: Which tool is specifically about tracking and saving changes over time?

contentSections.body:
**Step 1: Install VS Code**
Download from code.visualstudio.com. Run the installer. Open it.

Recommended extensions to install after:
- **Prettier** — Auto-formats your code on save (essential)
- **ESLint** — Highlights code quality issues

**Step 2: Install Node.js**
Download from nodejs.org — choose the LTS (Long Term Support) version. The installer also installs `npm`.

Verify it worked: open VS Code's terminal (Ctrl+` or Cmd+`) and run:
```
node --version
npm --version
```
Both should print version numbers.

**Step 3: Install git**
On Mac: run `git --version` in terminal — if not installed, macOS will prompt you to install it automatically.
On Windows: download from git-scm.com and run the installer.

**Low-energy shortcut:** If setup feels overwhelming today, use [Replit](https://replit.com) or [StackBlitz](https://stackblitz.com) — browser-based coding environments. No installation needed. You can always set up locally when you have more capacity.

The terminal is where you run commands. It looks scary. It's just typing.

The commands you'll use most:
```
pwd           # Where am I? (print working directory)
ls            # What's in this folder? (list)
cd foldername # Move into a folder (change directory)
cd ..         # Go up one folder
mkdir myapp   # Create a new folder
```

**Your first session:**
```bash
# Open VS Code terminal (Ctrl+` or Cmd+`)
cd Desktop           # Go to Desktop
mkdir my-first-app   # Create a folder
cd my-first-app      # Go into it
node --version       # Confirm Node is installed
```

If `node --version` prints something like `v20.10.0` — you're set up.

**Marcus's tip:** *"I kept a cheat sheet of terminal commands on my phone for the first month. Once you use them a few times they stick. The ones I still use every single day: `ls`, `cd`, and `git status`.*"
VS Code = editor. Node.js = run JavaScript. git = save history. Install in that order. Verify with `node --version`.

title: Terminal Basics
description: Navigate your filesystem. Run scripts. The terminal is just a chat app for your computer.

learningObjectives.text: Navigate directories using cd, ls, and pwd
Create and remove files and directories
Run a JavaScript file from the terminal using Node.js

contentSections.body: The terminal has a reputation for being scary. It's not. You know how to type in a search bar? The terminal is the same thing, but instead of searching the web, you're giving your computer direct instructions. No mouse. Just keyboard.

### Navigation commands (the ones you'll use daily):

| Command | What it does | Example |
|---------|-------------|----------|
| `pwd` | Show current folder | `pwd` → `/Users/sarah/Desktop` |
| `ls` | List files in current folder | `ls` |
| `ls -la` | List files with details (including hidden) | `ls -la` |
| `cd name` | Move into a folder | `cd my-project` |
| `cd ..` | Go up one folder | `cd ..` |
| `cd ~` | Go to home folder | `cd ~` |
| `mkdir name` | Create a new folder | `mkdir my-app` |
| `touch name` | Create an empty file | `touch index.js` |
| `rm name` | Delete a file ⚠️ | `rm old-file.js` |
| `rm -rf name` | Delete a folder ⚠️ | `rm -rf old-folder` |
**`rm` deletes permanently.** There is no trash can. Files deleted with `rm` are gone. Double-check before pressing Enter.

contentSections.question: You're in `/Users/sarah/Documents` and you want to get to `/Users/sarah/Desktop`. What commands do you run?
contentSections.answer:
```bash
cd ..          # Go up to /Users/sarah/
cd Desktop     # Go into Desktop
```
Or in one command:
```bash
cd ../Desktop
```
Or using absolute path:
```bash
cd ~/Desktop   # ~ is always your home folder
```
contentSections.hint: You need to go up one level first, then into the target folder.

contentSections.question: You want to write and run your first JavaScript file. Put these steps in order.
steps: mkdir my-first-app
cd my-first-app
touch hello.js
code .
Write console.log(...) in hello.js and save
node hello.js
contentSections.explanation: mkdir creates the folder, cd moves into it, touch creates the empty file, code . opens it in your editor, you write and save the code, then node hello.js actually runs it. Skip a step — like forgetting to cd into the new folder first — and you'll create files in the wrong place.

contentSections.body:
Here's the simplest thing you can do in the terminal: write a JavaScript file and run it.

**Step 1:** Create a file
```bash
mkdir my-first-app
cd my-first-app
touch hello.js
```

**Step 2:** Open it in VS Code
```bash
code .           # Opens VS Code in current folder
```

**Step 3:** Write something in hello.js
```javascript
console.log('Hello from the terminal!');
console.log('I am', 'a', 'coder', 'now.');
```

**Step 4:** Run it
```bash
node hello.js
```

You'll see:
```
Hello from the terminal!
I am a coder now.
```

You just ran your first JavaScript program. It doesn't matter that it's simple.

**`code .` is magic.** It opens VS Code in the current directory. If it doesn't work, open VS Code → Command Palette (Ctrl+Shift+P or Cmd+Shift+P) → type "Install 'code' command in PATH" → press Enter.

Two terminal shortcuts that save enormous time:

**Tab completion** — Start typing a folder or file name and press Tab. The terminal auto-completes it. Press Tab twice to see all options if multiple match.
```bash
cd Des[TAB]  →  cd Desktop/
```

**Command history** — Press the ↑ arrow to see your previous commands. Press ↑ multiple times to go further back. Press ↓ to come forward. You almost never need to retype a command.

**Windows note:** These commands use Unix syntax (Mac/Linux). On Windows, you can use PowerShell (which supports most Unix commands) or install Git Bash which gives you the full Unix terminal experience.
Navigate with `cd`, list with `ls`, create with `mkdir`/`touch`, run JavaScript with `node filename.js`. Tab and ↑ save you 50% of your typing.

title: What Are Variables?
description: Variables are labeled containers for data. Once you understand this, everything else follows.

learningObjectives.text: Define a variable and explain why they exist
Declare variables using const and let correctly
Explain the difference between const and let

contentSections.body: Sarah is building a habit tracker. The app needs to remember: the user's name, their streak count, the date of their last login, whether they've completed today's habit. Where does all of this *live*? In variables.

contentSections.answer:
`Hello, Marcus!`

The `+` operator joins strings together. This is called **string concatenation**. You're combining the value in `greeting`, then a literal `, `, then the value in `name`, then `!`.
contentSections.hint: Look at what's stored in each variable and how they're being combined.

contentSections.question: This code throws an error. Which line causes it?

options.label: const appName = 'HabitFlow';
appName = 'DifferentName';

feedback.line1: This line is fine — it's just declaring a new const.
feedback.line2: Right — this is the crash. You can't reassign a const after it's created.

contentSections.flawExplanation: const means the value can't be reassigned after creation. let is for values that need to change. Rule of thumb: use const by default, switch to let only when you know the value will change.

contentSections.body:
There are two main ways to declare variables: `const` and `let`.

**`let`** — The value can be changed.
```javascript
let streakDays = 0;
streakDays = 1;   // ✅ Fine
streakDays = 14;  // ✅ Fine
```

### The rule: **Use `const` by default. Use `let` when you know the value will change.**

```javascript
const userName = 'Sarah';        // Won't change — const
const appVersion = '1.0.0';      // Won't change — const
let currentStreak = 0;           // Will change — let
let isLoggedIn = false;          // Will change — let
```
**You might see `var` in older code.** `var` is the old way (pre-2015) and has confusing scoping behavior. Avoid it. Use `const` and `let`.
**When in doubt, be more descriptive.** `isHabitCompletedToday` is better than `completed`. Your future self (and future Claude sessions) will thank you.
Variables = labeled containers for data. Use `const` by default, `let` when values change. Name them descriptively — code is read by humans.

title: Data Types
description: String, number, boolean. Not all data is the same. The difference matters more than you'd expect.

learningObjectives.text: Identify the five basic JavaScript data types
Explain why type matters when performing operations
Predict the result of operations that mix types

contentSections.body: Alex writes `42 + '8'` in the console. What comes back surprises him — and it's the source of some of the most confusing bugs in JavaScript.

contentSections.question: What type is `'42'`? What type is `42`? Are they the same?
contentSections.answer:
`'42'` is a **String** (text wrapped in quotes).
`42` is a **Number**.

They are NOT the same. `'42' === 42` is `false`. JavaScript sees them as completely different things. This is why `42 + '8'` gives `'428'` — JavaScript converts the number to a string and *concatenates* them instead of adding.
contentSections.hint: Look at whether there are quote marks around the 42.

contentSections.scenario:
```javascript
42 + '8'
```
contentSections.question: What does this evaluate to?

options.label: NaN

feedback.50: That's what you'd get if both sides were numbers — but '8' here is a string, not a number.
feedback.428: Right. JavaScript converts the number 42 to the string '42', then concatenates: '42' + '8' → '428'.
feedback.nan: JS doesn't give up and bail to NaN here — it finds a way to combine them, just not the way you'd expect.

contentSections.concept: **Type coercion**: when an operator's two sides don't match types, JavaScript automatically converts one of them rather than throwing an error. `+` with a string on either side triggers string concatenation, so the number gets turned into text first.

contentSections.body:
JavaScript will automatically convert types in some operations. This is called **type coercion** and it's responsible for many confusing bugs.

```javascript
// Number + String = String concatenation
5 + '3'     // → '53' (not 8!)

// Number - String = Number subtraction (weird but true)
'10' - 5    // → 5 (JS converts '10' to 10)

// Boolean to Number
true + 1    // → 2 (true becomes 1)
false + 1   // → 1 (false becomes 0)

// Comparison gotchas
0 == false  // → true  (loose equality, converts types)
0 === false // → false (strict equality, no conversion)
```

**The fix: always use `===` (triple equals)** for comparisons. It never coerces types.

**Always use `===` not `==`.** The double equals (`==`) does type coercion and produces surprising results. Triple equals (`===`) compares both value AND type. In 5 years of coding you'll rarely need `==`.

### Check the type of a value:
```javascript
typeof 'hello'     // → 'string'
typeof 42          // → 'number'
typeof true        // → 'boolean'
typeof null        // → 'object' ← infamous bug, null is NOT an object
typeof undefined   // → 'undefined'
```

### Convert between types explicitly:
```javascript
// String to Number
Number('42')          // → 42
parseInt('42px', 10)  // → 42 (extracts number from string)
parseFloat('3.14')    // → 3.14

// Number to String
String(42)            // → '42'
(42).toString()       // → '42'

// Anything to Boolean
Boolean(0)            // → false
Boolean('')           // → false (empty string is falsy)
Boolean('hello')      // → true
Boolean(1)            // → true
```
**Falsy values in JavaScript:** `0`, `''`, `null`, `undefined`, `NaN`, and `false` all behave like `false` in conditions. Everything else is truthy. This is useful shorthand but can be surprising.
String/Number/Boolean/null/undefined are the five basic types. Use `===` for comparisons. Convert types explicitly when needed with `Number()`, `String()`, etc.

title: Working with Variables
description: Operations, template literals, and your first real JavaScript expressions.

learningObjectives.text: Perform arithmetic and string operations on variables
Use template literals to combine variables with text
Store the result of an expression in a new variable

contentSections.body: Marcus is tracking his job applications. He applied to 12 companies, got 3 phone screens, and wants to know his conversion rate. Let's calculate that.
**`%` is modulo** — the remainder after division. `10 % 3` = `1` (10 divided by 3 is 3 remainder 1). Useful for checking if a number is even: `if (n % 2 === 0)` means n is even.

contentSections.answer:
`You have 5 items. Total: €17.5`

The expression `${items * price}` is evaluated inside the template literal. You can put any JavaScript expression inside `${}` — not just variable names.
contentSections.hint: JavaScript evaluates everything inside ${ } before building the string.

contentSections.body:
A few operations you'll use constantly:

**Math:**
```javascript
Math.round(3.7)     // → 4
Math.floor(3.9)     // → 3 (always rounds down)
Math.ceil(3.1)      // → 4 (always rounds up)
Math.max(1, 5, 3)   // → 5
Math.min(1, 5, 3)   // → 1
Math.random()       // → random decimal between 0 and 1
```

**Strings:**
```javascript
const name = 'sarah';
name.length           // → 5
name.toUpperCase()    // → 'SARAH'
name.includes('ar')   // → true
name.replace('sarah', 'SARAH')  // → 'SARAH'
name.trim()           // removes spaces from start/end
```
**`console.log()` is your best friend.** When you're not sure what a value is, log it. `console.log('the streak is:', streakDays)` prints to the terminal. Use it constantly while learning.
Use arithmetic operators for math, template literals (backticks + `${}`) for building strings. `console.log()` everything when debugging.

title: If/Else Decisions
description: Every decision your app makes is an if/else. Learn to write conditions that work every time.

learningObjectives.text: Write an if/else statement that evaluates a condition
Combine conditions using && and ||
Choose between if/else and the ternary operator appropriately

contentSections.body: "If user is logged in, show dashboard. Otherwise, show login page." If the streak is over 7 days, show a special badge. If the form is empty, show an error. **If/else is how code makes decisions.**

contentSections.answer:
`Getting there!`

5 is NOT >= 7, so the first condition fails. 5 IS >= 3, so the second condition passes. JavaScript stops checking and runs that branch. The `else` block is never reached.
contentSections.hint: JavaScript checks each condition in order and runs the FIRST one that's true.

contentSections.question: isLoggedIn is true. streakDays is 5. What runs?

options.label: showStreakBadge() runs
'No badge yet' is logged

feedback.nobadge: Right. `&&` needs **both** sides to be true. `isLoggedIn` is true, but `streakDays >= 7` is false — 5 is less than 7. One false side is enough to make the whole condition false, so the `else` branch runs.
feedback.badge: Not quite. `&&` needs **both** sides to be true, not just one. `isLoggedIn` is true, but `streakDays >= 7` is false — 5 is less than 7. Since one side is false, the whole condition is false, so the `else` branch runs instead.

contentSections.body: **Parentheses control order.** `(A && B) || C` is different from `A && (B || C)`. When in doubt, add parentheses to make your intent explicit.
**Avoid nested ternaries.** `a ? b ? c : d : e` — nobody can read this. If you need nested conditions, use if/else.
if/else controls program flow. Use `&&` for AND, `||` for OR, `!` for NOT. Use ternary for simple one-line value assignments.

title: Loops — Do It Again
description: Loops let you repeat code without rewriting it. Essential for working with lists of data.

learningObjectives.text: Use a for loop to repeat code a known number of times
Use forEach to iterate over an array
Use map to transform an array into a new one

contentSections.body: Sarah has a list of 30 habits. Without loops, displaying them would require writing 30 identical lines of code. With loops, it's 4 lines. This is why loops are one of the most important concepts in programming.

contentSections.question: How many times does console.log run in total?
contentSections.explanation: habits.length is 4, and the loop condition i < habits.length keeps it running for i = 0, 1, 2, 3 — four passes, one per item in the array. This is exactly why loops over arrays almost always start at i = 0 and compare against .length.

contentSections.question: The loop `for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++)` — how many times does it run? What are the values of `i`?
contentSections.answer:
It runs **3 times**. The values of `i` are `0`, `1`, `2`.

Note: it starts at `0` and stops **before** reaching `3`. Arrays also start at index 0, which is why loops over arrays often start at `i = 0`.
contentSections.hint: Count the values: when does i start, when does the condition become false?

contentSections.title: forEach and map — the modern way

contentSections.body: **In React, you'll use `map()` constantly.** `array.map((item) => <Component key={item.id} data={item} />)` is how you render lists in React. Master `map()` and 30% of React becomes intuitive.

**The pattern you'll see everywhere:** `array.filter(...).map(...)` — filter down to what you need, then transform it. Sarah's habit tracker: `habits.filter(h => h.completed).map(h => h.name)` → get names of all completed habits.
`for` loops repeat code N times. `forEach` runs code per item. `map` transforms items. `filter` keeps matching items. `find` gets the first match.

title: Your First Function
description: Functions are reusable blocks of code. The foundation of every larger program.

learningObjectives.text: Explain why functions exist and when to create one
Write a function with parameters and a return value
Call a function and use its return value

contentSections.body: Sarah notices she's writing the same streak-calculation code in three different places in her app. Then she finds a bug. Now she has to fix it in three places. She misses one. Users see wrong streak counts. **Functions solve this.**

contentSections.scenario: Sarah notices she's writing the same streak-calculation code in three different places in her app. Then she finds a bug. Now she has to fix it in three places. She misses one. Users see wrong streak counts.
contentSections.question: What's actually going wrong here?

options.label: She's not careful enough while coding
The same logic is duplicated across the codebase

feedback.careful: Carefulness isn't really the issue — even a careful developer will eventually miss one of three copies when fixing a bug. The setup itself is the problem.
feedback.duplication: Right. The same logic living in three places means every future fix has to happen three times, correctly, every time. Miss one and you get exactly this bug.

contentSections.mechanism: A function is a named, reusable block of code. You define it once, call it many times — so a fix only ever has to happen in one place.

contentSections.answer:
`80`

Step by step:
1. `discount = 100 * (20 / 100)` = `100 * 0.2` = `20`
2. `return 100 - 20` = `80`

The function takes two **parameters** (`price` and `percentOff`) as inputs, does the math, and **returns** the result.
contentSections.hint: Follow the math step by step. What is 20% of 100? Then subtract.

contentSections.body: **`return` exits immediately.** The moment JavaScript hits a `return`, it stops running the function and gives back that value. Anything after a `return` is unreachable.
**Rule of thumb:** If you can't describe what a function does in one sentence without using "and", it probably does too much. Split it up.
Functions = reusable named blocks of code. Parameters are inputs; `return` is the output. Use them to avoid repetition and keep code organized.

title: Instructions, written by humans, for humans
description: What code actually is — an exact instruction with no room for a computer to guess what you meant — and why the people who write it still write it for other humans too.

learningObjectives.text: Explain that code is a sequence of exact instructions a computer follows literally, never intuitively
Distinguish an instruction a computer could act on from one that silently relies on human judgment
Recognise that code is written for future human readers as much as for the machine

contentSections.title: A computer does exactly what you typed, not what you meant

contentSections.body: You're in bed, and you text your partner: "Can you grab my charger?" They come back with the laptop charger. You meant the phone one. There are three chargers in this house and your sentence didn't rule out two of them — a person filled the gap with a guess. A computer doesn't have a guessing instinct to fall back on. It would need to know which charger, on which nightstand, in which room, or it does nothing at all.

contentSections.scenario: You want a plant watered. You could tell your housemate: **"Water the plant if it's dry."** You could tell a program: **"If soil moisture reads below 30%, run the pump for 3 seconds."** You could also just say: **"Take care of the plant while I'm out."**
contentSections.question: Which of these could you hand directly to a computer, with no follow-up questions needed?

options.label: "Water the plant if it's dry"
"If soil moisture reads below 30%, run the pump for 3 seconds"
"Take care of the plant while I'm out"

feedback.housemate: This one sounds precise, and it works fine on a human — but "dry" is a judgment call. Dry compared to what? A computer has no built-in sense of dry; it needs a number and a threshold before it can check anything.
feedback.sensor: Right. This names an exact measurable check (a moisture reading, a number) and an exact action (run the pump, for a stated time). There is nothing left for the computer to interpret.
feedback.vague: This is the vaguest of the three, which is useful for noticing the pattern: it asks for a whole area of judgment ("take care of") rather than a single checkable action. A computer given this instruction has no idea what to even attempt.

contentSections.concept: A computer only ever does what a specific, checkable rule tells it to do — there's no in-between step where it applies judgment. "If it's dry" has to become "if moisture reads below a number" before a machine can act on it. That translation, from what you mean to a rule a machine can check, is most of what writing code actually is.

contentSections.body: This is the whole difference between everyday language and a programming language. English (or any spoken language) is full of small gaps a listener fills in automatically without noticing — tone, context, "you know what I mean." A computer has none of that. Programming languages exist specifically to remove the gaps: every value has to be named, every condition has to be exact, every step has to be spelled out in the order it happens. That isn't the computer being difficult. It's the actual shape of the tool.
Code isn't smarter than plain language — it's plain language with all the guessing removed.

You write a few lines of code at 2am because it's the only quiet hour you've had all week. Three weeks later you open the same file, foggy, needing to change one thing, with zero memory of why you wrote it that way. The computer never had that problem. You do.

contentSections.question: Code only has to be exact enough for a computer to run. So why do experienced programmers spend real time worrying about whether a human could read it?
contentSections.hint: Think about who actually opens a file again after it's already working.
contentSections.answer: Because the computer is not the only reader. Code gets reopened, by its author with less memory than they have right now, or by someone else entirely, far more often than it gets written the first time — and a version that only the computer can parse is a version that costs real time to safely change later.

contentSections.body: Code has two audiences at once: the computer, which needs exactness, and future humans, who need clarity. Meeting the computer's requirement is not optional — the program won't run otherwise. Meeting the human requirement is a choice you make every time you name a value something specific instead of `x`, or leave a short note explaining *why* a line does something unusual (not *what* it does — the code already says what; a comment earns its place by saying why).
You will read this code again with less context than you have right now. Write it for that version of you.

title: What actually happens when you run a program
description: The mechanical path from clicking Run to seeing a result, and why a program always executes one line at a time, in the order you wrote them.

learningObjectives.text: Describe, at a high level, the path from typed code to a visible result
Explain why a program runs top-to-bottom by default
Predict what happens when a later line's setup is needed by an earlier one

contentSections.title: From your keyboard to the screen

contentSections.body: You type three lines of code, click Run, and text appears. That gap — between the click and the text — feels like it could be anything. It's actually one small, boring, repeatable habit, done very fast.

contentSections.question: Put these in the order they actually happen when you run a program.
steps: You type code into a file
You click Run (or type a command that means the same thing)
The JavaScript engine starts at the top of the file
It reads the next line, translates it, and does exactly what it says
It moves to the following line and repeats, until there are no lines left
Whatever the code told it to display — text, a number — appears on screen
contentSections.explanation: Nothing in this chain is mysterious once it's laid out — the only part that varies is what each individual line asks for. The engine's job is always the same: read the next instruction, execute it exactly, move to the next one.

contentSections.body: The "engine" here — for JavaScript, this is what your browser or Node.js runs — doesn't understand your program the way you understand a paragraph. It reads one line, converts it into something the machine's hardware can act on, carries that out, and only then looks at the next line. It never skips ahead, never reorders for convenience, and never does two lines "at once." That single-minded, one-thing-at-a-time habit is the entire mechanism. Nothing more clever is happening underneath.
Running a program is: read the next line, do exactly what it says, repeat until there are no more lines.

Swap two lines of a working program and it can stop working entirely — not because the swapped lines were individually wrong, but because one of them now needs something the other hasn't provided yet.

contentSections.question: What's actually going wrong here?

options.label: The math itself is wrong
`total` is being used on a line that runs before it's created
`console.log` can't print numbers, only text

feedback.math: The arithmetic is fine — 4.50 + 2.25 + 6.00 would total correctly, if the program ever got that far. The problem happens before any math runs.
feedback.order: Right. At the moment the first line runs, `total` doesn't exist yet — the line that creates it is still below, waiting its turn. The computer has no way to reach ahead and grab a value that hasn't been set up yet.
feedback.printtype: `console.log` prints numbers fine — that's not the failure here. Nothing about the print function itself is the issue.

contentSections.mechanism: Every line depends on every line above it having already run. There's no simultaneous execution and no lookahead — a variable has to be created before any line can use it. Reordering these two lines (create `total` first, print it second) fixes it completely, because it matches the order the computer actually needs things in.

contentSections.body: This is worth sitting with because it explains a huge share of a beginner's first errors: not bad logic, but logic written in an order the computer can't follow yet. A grocery total has to be calculated before it can be announced. A name has to be collected before it can be greeted. If a line needs a value, something above it has to have already created that value — the computer will never go looking ahead on your behalf.
Nothing runs at the same time. If a line needs something from an earlier line, that earlier line has to run first.

title: Languages: why there are so many and why it barely matters yet
description: Programming languages differ in vocabulary and punctuation, not in the underlying ideas — and picking one and finishing something beats sampling five.

learningObjectives.text: Explain that programming languages differ in syntax but share the same underlying logic
Recognise that most beginner concepts transfer across languages
Decide not to restart in a new language over an ordinary early mistake

contentSections.body: You ask an AI tool to write you something and it answers in Python. A friend's tutorial uses JavaScript. A job posting mentions a third one. You start to worry you picked "the wrong one" before you've written a single working line.

contentSections.question: Which of these is the "more correct" way to print Hello three times?

options.label: The JavaScript one
The Python one
Neither — they do the same thing

feedback.js: It's not wrong to prefer it, but "more correct" isn't a real category here — both programs do exactly the same job, with different punctuation.
feedback.py: Same issue in the other direction: Python isn't more correct for doing the identical thing with fewer symbols. Fewer symbols is a style choice, not a correctness one.
feedback.same: Right. Both loop three times and print "Hello" each time. The curly braces, the semicolons, the word `for` versus indentation — all of that is dialect. The idea underneath ("repeat this three times") is identical.

contentSections.concept: Every language argues about its own punctuation — brackets, indentation, keywords. None of them disagree about whether "repeat an action a fixed number of times" is a real, useful thing to be able to say. That underlying move is called a loop, and it exists, in some spelling, in every general-purpose language.

contentSections.body: This holds for the handful of ideas that actually carry a beginner course: storing a value under a name, repeating something, checking a condition and branching based on it, grouping steps into a named, reusable block. Every mainstream language has all four. What changes between languages is the vocabulary and the punctuation used to say them — not whether the ideas exist. Learning any one language properly means you've already learned most of what the next one needs; you're mainly relearning spelling.
Every language argues about punctuation. None of them argue about whether "do this three times" is a real idea.
You've read six "best language for beginners" articles and haven't opened an editor yet. Somewhere in there, comparing options quietly became a substitute for starting.

contentSections.scenario: This course teaches JavaScript first. Not because it's the only viable choice — because a choice had to be made, and this one has specific, defensible reasons behind it.
contentSections.question: Which of these are genuinely good reasons to start with JavaScript, as opposed to reasons that sound good but don't hold up?

items.label: It runs in any web browser with nothing to install first
It's used in both websites and a lot of backend and tooling work
It's objectively the fastest programming language to execute
It's the only language good enough for a real programmer to use

explanation.browser: True and genuinely useful for a beginner in bed on a phone: you can start writing and running code with zero setup, before Module 2 even gets to installing anything.
explanation.range: Also true — the same language you're learning shows up in a very wide range of real jobs later, so the time invested here keeps paying off.
explanation.fastest: Not true, and not really the point either way. Raw execution speed is close to irrelevant for a beginner's first hundred programs.
explanation.only: False, and worth naming directly: there is no one language "real" programmers use. Professionals use dozens, chosen per job. The idea that one language is the serious one and the rest are lesser is a myth that mostly produces language-shopping instead of learning.

contentSections.synthesis: The real reasons are practical (nothing to install, wide later use), not mythical (fastest, only real one). That's worth knowing, because the mythical reasons are exactly the kind of thing that make someone abandon a working start over.

contentSections.body: Skills transfer more than beginners expect. Once storing values, repeating, and branching on a condition actually click, a second language mostly asks you to relearn vocabulary, not relearn the ideas from zero. The real cost isn't picking the "wrong" language — it's restarting the syntax-learning clock every time doubt shows up, which quietly means never finishing anything long enough to see the ideas click at all.
Finishing something small in one language teaches you more than sampling five.

title: The gap between knowing and doing, and how to close it
description: Why reading and watching don't produce the ability to write code, and how to pick an action small enough to actually close that gap today.

learningObjectives.text: Explain why reading or watching about code doesn't transfer into writing it
Identify the smallest next action that would close the knowing-doing gap today
Recognise passive-consumption habits that feel like learning but aren't

contentSections.body: You've watched four hours of coding videos this week and nodded along the whole time. Then you open a blank editor to try it yourself and don't know how to type the first line. Nothing about the four hours prepared you for the specific problem the blank page presents.

contentSections.question: Why does watching someone else code feel like real progress, even when it doesn't transfer to your own blank editor?
contentSections.hint: Think about the difference between recognizing the right answer on a multiple-choice test and having to produce it yourself from a blank page.
contentSections.answer: Watching lets you recognize the next step the instant it's shown to you — your brain confirms "yes, that makes sense" and moves on, which genuinely feels like understanding. Writing from a blank page requires generating that same step yourself, with nothing prompting you. Recognition and recall are different skills, and only one of them is what a blank editor actually tests.

contentSections.body: This isn't a case against tutorials — they're a reasonable way to see what's possible and pick up vocabulary. The trap is treating watching as a substitute for typing. A useful rule of thumb: for every chunk of video or reading, spend at least as long typing and running something yourself, even if it's a tiny, ugly, three-line copy with one thing changed. That's the part that actually builds the skill a blank editor is going to ask for.
Watching someone cook doesn't make your hands know how to chop. Neither does watching someone code.
You have about fifteen minutes and low energy tonight, and somewhere there's a whole "learn to code" checklist looming that you have no intention of finishing right now.

contentSections.intro: Not every practice session needs to be big. Build the shape of a session small enough to actually happen tonight.

options: Something that takes an evening
Something that takes under 10 minutes
Something with no clear end point
fields.correctValue: Something that takes under 10 minutes
fields.feedback: An evening-sized plan is a plan for a good day only. Under 10 minutes is small enough to survive most days — and a real 10 minutes beats a planned, unstarted hour every time.

fields.prompt: What should be true when it's done?
options: A vague sense of having "reviewed something"
Something you can point to on screen — a line that ran, an error you actually read
fields.correctValue: Something you can point to on screen — a line that ran, an error you actually read
fields.feedback: A visible result is checkable. "I reviewed something" has no finish line, which makes it easy to quietly not happen at all.

fields.prompt: When do you decide to start?
options: Wait until you feel motivated enough
Open the editor before deciding how you feel about it
fields.correctValue: Open the editor before deciding how you feel about it
fields.feedback: Waiting for motivation hands the decision to a feeling that's often absent on exactly the days a small win would help most. Opening the editor first, before judging the feeling, sidesteps that.

contentSections.synthesis: Put together: a task under 10 minutes, with a visible result, started before you've decided how you feel about it. That's a session small enough to actually survive a real week — including the bad days in it.

contentSections.body: The gap between knowing and doing doesn't close with one big study session; it closes with a lot of small real actions that are actually completed. A tiny action finished tonight teaches more than a large one postponed to "when I have more energy," because postponed sessions have a way of costing nothing right up until they cost the whole habit.
The gap between knowing and doing closes one tiny real action at a time, never one big study session.

title: Learning to code with a body that has opinions
description: Building a coding practice around variable capacity instead of a fixed plan that only survives good days — and deciding, in advance, what still counts on a bad one.

learningObjectives.text: Adapt a coding practice session to today's actual energy rather than a fixed plan
Identify which parts of a session to preserve versus skip on a low-capacity day
Build a personal minimum viable session for low-capacity days, decided in advance

contentSections.title: Capacity, not discipline, is the variable

contentSections.body: You planned an hour of practice. You wake up foggy, everything's too loud, and sitting up isn't happening today. Nothing about last night's plan accounted for this morning.

contentSections.scenario: Two learners hit the exact same bad week. One quietly stops the track entirely — the plan didn't survive contact with a rough few days. The other does five minutes on the worst day instead of the planned hour, and picks the hour back up once capacity returns.
contentSections.question: What actually determined the difference between them?

options.label: How disciplined each person is
How well the plan bends when capacity drops
How naturally talented each person is at coding

feedback.discipline: It's tempting to read it this way, but both learners hit identical circumstances — the difference wasn't willpower, it was whether either plan had a smaller version built in to fall back on.
feedback.bend: Right. A plan with a real low-capacity version survives a bad week by shrinking instead of breaking. A plan without one only has two states: the full version, or nothing — and "nothing" is what a bad day forces if that's the only alternative on offer.
feedback.talent: Neither learner's outcome had anything to do with how naturally coding comes to them — this was entirely about what happened during a rough stretch, before either of them had written much code at all.

contentSections.concept: A fixed high-effort plan breaks the first time capacity genuinely drops, because it never designed for that. A plan with a defined, smaller "still counts" version survives the same drop, because dropping capacity was already accounted for rather than treated as a failure to push through.

contentSections.body: This isn't specific to coding, but it matters here because a coding habit dies quietly — there's no single dramatic quit moment, just a string of skipped sessions that never quite restart. Building the low-capacity version of a plan on a decent day, rather than inventing it mid-crash, is what keeps a session possible on the days that actually threaten the habit.
A plan that only works on good days isn't a plan — it's a bet that you'll keep having good days.
The best time to decide what a bad-day session looks like is on a day you have the capacity to decide it — not in the middle of one, when deciding anything at all is the hardest part.

contentSections.scenario: You're sketching your own minimum viable session — the smallest thing that still counts as practice on your worst realistic day.
contentSections.question: Which of these belong in a genuinely usable bad-day plan?

items.label: Reread one paragraph of your notes from last time
Type and run one line of code, even if you copy it from earlier work
Finish the whole exercise set before stopping, no matter what
Decide the actual next action while you still have the energy to decide, not once the bad day has already started

explanation.reread: Small, low-effort, and it keeps the thread from last session from going completely cold — a genuinely reasonable bad-day action.
explanation.oneline: Yes — this is small enough to survive real fog and still counts as practice, because it keeps the physical habit of opening the editor alive.
explanation.finishset: This is exactly the kind of item that turns a bad-day plan back into a good-day plan in disguise. "The whole set, no matter what" has no smaller version, which means a bad enough day just skips it.
explanation.decidebefore: This is the one that actually makes the other two possible — deciding what "still counts" looks like on a day you have the energy to decide it, so a bad day doesn't have to invent a plan from nothing.

contentSections.synthesis: A real minimum viable session is small, has a visible result, and was decided in advance — on a day capacity allowed for deciding, not on the day it's needed.

contentSections.body: Decide what counts as "still practicing" before the bad day arrives, not during it.

title: Practice — Predict What Eight Tiny Programs Will Print
description: Eight drills, no new concepts: reading a few lines of JavaScript and correctly predicting exactly what will appear on screen, before running anything.

learningObjectives.text: Trace a short program's execution line by line and predict its exact output

contentSections.body: Every one of these is small enough to hold in your head at once. The skill being drilled isn't cleverness — it's the habit of tracing top to bottom, one line at a time, before assuming you already know the answer.
Reading code accurately, before running it, is most of what debugging will turn out to be later.

title: Lab — Write Down What You Want to Build By the End
description: Turn vague wishes about learning to code into three specific, small, personally meaningful build goals you can return to across the rest of the track.

learningObjectives.text: Turn a vague coding wish into a build specific enough to plan for
Explain, in personal terms, why each goal matters to you specifically
Write a goal statement that accounts honestly for variable capacity

contentSections.body: "I want to learn to code" is a wish, not a target — it's exactly the kind of instruction lesson 1 said a computer couldn't act on, and it turns out you can't act on it very well either. This lab produces something more useful: three specific things you'd actually like to build, and why each one is yours.

contentSections.title: Three things you'd like to build
contentSections.brief: By the end of this track you'll have built small, real programs. Right now, before any of the syntax is in place, is the right time to write down *what for* — not because the goals are fixed forever, but because a specific target changes how the next 100 hours feel, from "studying" to "working toward something."
contentSections.deliverable: A written goal with three things you'd like to make, and why each one matters to you.

stages.title: Notice code you already use
stages.instructions: List five things you interact with regularly that are, underneath, someone's code: a reminder app, a spreadsheet that calculates totals, a form that validates an email address, a game, a bot that replies to messages. For each, write one sentence on what it actually does, mechanically — not what it's for, but what steps it must be running.
stages.checkpoint: You have five real examples, each with one sentence describing its underlying mechanics rather than its purpose.

stages.title: Turn three vague wishes into three specific builds
stages.instructions: Write three things you'd like to build. For each, apply lesson 1's test: is this specific enough that a computer (or you, later) could start on it with no further questions? "An app for my meds" isn't there yet. "A page where I type a med name and time, and it lists everything for today" is. Push each of your three past the vague version.
stages.checkpoint: Each of your three ideas is small enough to imagine actually finishing, and specific enough that a stranger reading it would know exactly what it does.

stages.title: Say why each one is actually yours
stages.instructions: For each of the three, write one or two sentences on why it matters to you personally — not "it would be useful" in general, but the specific situation in your life it responds to. This is the part that keeps a goal alive on a low-motivation day, so don't skip it or make it generic.
stages.checkpoint: Each build has a real, specific reason attached that's about your actual life, not a generic justification that could belong to anyone.

stages.title: Order them and write the goal statement
stages.instructions: Put your three builds in the order you'd actually attempt them, with one sentence on why that order. Then write a short paragraph (4-6 sentences) that states all three, in order, and includes one sentence about what happens to this plan on a bad week — because lesson 5 was about exactly that, and a goal with no bad-week clause is a goal for good weeks only.
stages.checkpoint: You have one paragraph naming all three builds in order, with reasoning for the order, and an explicit sentence about what a bad week does to the plan.

rubric.criterion: Each build idea is specific enough to start
rubric.meets: Reads like "a page that adds up my grocery list", not "an app" — a stranger could picture what it does.

rubric.criterion: Each idea says why it matters to you personally
rubric.meets: Names a real situation in your life, not a generic benefit anyone could claim.

rubric.criterion: The three are ordered, with reasoning
rubric.meets: States which comes first and why, not just a list in whatever order they were written.

rubric.criterion: The goal statement has a bad-week clause
rubric.meets: Explicitly says what happens to the plan on a low-capacity week, not just what happens on a good one.

rubric.criterion: It's honest about being a beginner goal
rubric.meets: None of the three require skills the track hasn't gotten to yet — they're realistic starting points, not finished-programmer fantasies.

contentSections.body: A specific goal, written down before you know how to build it, is what turns the next 99 and a half hours from studying into working toward something.

title: Checkpoint — What Code Actually Is
description: Ten questions pulling from this module. Ungraded, untimed — getting one wrong just means it comes back in a later checkpoint.

learningObjectives.text: Retrieve this module's core distinctions without looking them up

questions.from: This module — What Code Actually Is
questions.prompt: What makes an instruction something a computer can actually act on?

options.label: It's polite and clearly worded
It's exact enough that nothing is left for judgment
It's written in a real programming language, regardless of vagueness

questions.explanation: Exactness is the requirement, not politeness or which language it's written in. "If moisture reads below 30%" works because there's no gap left to fill with judgment; "if it's dry" doesn't, in any language.

questions.from: This module — What Code Actually Is
questions.prompt: Besides the computer, who is code actually written for?

options.label: Nobody else — the computer is the only real reader
Future humans, including the same person who wrote it, later, with less context
Only teammates who will review it

questions.explanation: The person most likely to reopen a piece of code is its own author, weeks later, with less memory of it than they have right now. Writing for that reader is a practical habit, not a courtesy.

questions.from: This module — What Code Actually Is
questions.prompt: In what order does a program's lines actually run?

options.label: Whichever order the computer decides is most efficient
Top to bottom, one line at a time, in the order they're written
All at once

questions.explanation: One line at a time, top to bottom, with nothing running simultaneously and no lookahead. This single habit is the entire mechanism behind how a program executes.

questions.from: This module — What Code Actually Is
questions.prompt: A line uses a variable that a later line creates. What happens?

options.label: It works fine — the computer reads the whole file first
It breaks, because that variable doesn't exist yet at that point in execution
It prints an empty value silently and continues

questions.explanation: The computer only knows what's already happened by the time a given line runs. A line can only use something an earlier line already set up — there's no reaching ahead.

questions.from: This module — What Code Actually Is
questions.prompt: What's actually different between programming languages, in most beginner-relevant cases?

options.label: The underlying logic — loops, conditions, and storage work completely differently
Mostly vocabulary and punctuation, while the core ideas stay the same
Nothing at all — every language is functionally identical

questions.explanation: Repetition, storing values, and branching on conditions exist in essentially every general-purpose language. What differs is the spelling — keywords, punctuation, syntax — not whether the ideas are there.

questions.from: This module — What Code Actually Is
questions.prompt: Why isn't restarting in a "better" language usually the right response to your first real error?

options.label: Because switching languages is against the rules of this course
Because that category of error exists in every language, and restarting mainly costs the syntax fluency you'd already built
Because every language error is identical in every language anyway

questions.explanation: Most early errors are logic-level, not language-specific — they'd happen in the new language too. Restarting doesn't remove the error category; it just resets your syntax progress.

questions.from: This module — What Code Actually Is
questions.prompt: Why doesn't watching a tutorial transfer well to writing code from a blank editor?

options.label: Tutorials are usually low quality
Watching trains recognizing the next step; writing requires generating it from nothing, which is a different skill
It transfers fine, actually, given enough total hours

questions.explanation: Recognition and recall are different skills. A blank editor tests recall specifically, and only typing and running your own code practices that.

questions.from: This module — What Code Actually Is
questions.prompt: What makes a "next action" small enough to actually happen on a bad day?

options.label: It should be scheduled for whenever you feel motivated
It's small, has a visible result, and gets started before you judge how you feel about it
It should match the size of your best day's session, for consistency

questions.explanation: Waiting for motivation hands the decision to a feeling that's often missing on hard days. Sizing the action for your worst realistic day, with a visible finish line, is what actually survives a real week.

questions.from: This module — What Code Actually Is
questions.prompt: What determines whether a coding habit survives a genuinely bad week?

options.label: How disciplined the learner is
Whether the plan has a real, smaller version built in for low-capacity days
Natural talent for coding

questions.explanation: A fixed high-effort plan breaks the first time capacity drops, because it has no smaller state to fall back into. A plan with a defined minimum version bends instead of breaking.

questions.from: This module — What Code Actually Is
questions.prompt: When should you decide what a bad-day coding session looks like?

options.label: In the moment, once the bad day has already started
On a day you have the capacity to decide, in advance
It doesn't need deciding — just do less, however that ends up looking

questions.explanation: Deciding a genuine minimum version on a good day means a bad day doesn't have to invent a plan from nothing — which is exactly when deciding anything is hardest.

contentSections.body: Anything that didn't come back will return in a later checkpoint. That's the design, not a failure.

title: Browser-based editors: coding with nothing installed
description: Starting to code tonight, on whatever device is in reach, using an editor that runs entirely in the browser — what it gives you, and its real tradeoffs.

learningObjectives.text: Use a browser-based editor to write and run code with nothing installed
Explain that browser-based editors are real coding tools, not a lesser substitute
Identify the genuine tradeoffs of a browser-based setup versus an installed one

contentSections.title: Nothing to install, coding from your phone in bed

contentSections.body: It's late, you're propped up on pillows, and the laptop is across the room where it might as well be on the moon. Your phone is right here. The question of whether you can code tonight turns out to hinge entirely on one thing: does anything need installing first?

contentSections.scenario: Two paths to writing your first line of code tonight. **Path A:** open a browser-based editor (a website that lets you write and run code directly in the page) and start typing. **Path B:** download an installed code editor, wait for it to install, then open it and start typing.
contentSections.question: Which path is realistic for tonight, on a phone, with low battery and low energy?

options.label: Path A — the browser-based editor
Path B — install something first
Neither — phones can't really run code

feedback.browser: Right. There's no download, no install, no waiting — you open a page in the browser you already have open, and the code you type runs on a server somewhere else. Your phone just needs to display a page and send your keystrokes.
feedback.install: Installing gets you real value eventually (lesson 2), but it costs time, storage, and often a laptop rather than a phone — exactly the things in shortest supply tonight.
feedback.neither: Phones run browsers, and browsers can run a browser-based editor just fine — the code itself executes on a remote server, not on the phone's own limited resources.

contentSections.concept: A browser-based editor runs almost entirely somewhere else — a server you connect to over the internet. Your device just needs a browser and a connection; it isn't doing the heavy lifting itself. That's what makes it available on a phone, a tablet, a borrowed laptop, or anything with a browser, with zero setup time.

contentSections.body: This matters more than it might sound like, because "I'll set it up properly this weekend" is exactly the kind of plan that depends on a good day showing up on schedule. A browser-based editor removes that dependency entirely for your first weeks: no install, no waiting for a good day with a laptop and a clear hour. You can start now, on whatever's in reach.
The fastest way to start coding tonight is the option with nothing to install.

contentSections.title: What you give up, and when it's worth it

contentSections.body: Halfway through a session, the connection drops for a second and the page shows a spinner. That's the honest tradeoff of a browser-based editor — it's real, but it's not the whole story.

contentSections.scenario: You're deciding how much to rely on a browser-based editor for the next few weeks.
contentSections.question: Which of these are genuine tradeoffs worth knowing about?

items.label: Nothing to install, works on any device with a browser
It's always faster to use than an installed editor
It needs an internet connection to save your work or run code
Free tiers can come with limits — private projects, how long code can run — worth checking before relying on it entirely

explanation.install: This is the real advantage, and it's a genuine one, not a consolation prize — zero setup time, works on whatever device is actually in reach.
explanation.faster: Not necessarily true, and not the point either way. An installed editor can feel snappier once it's set up, but that's a minor difference next to "available right now versus not."
explanation.internet: A real limitation. No connection means no editor, no saving, no running code — worth knowing before you're relying on it during a connectivity gap.
explanation.freetier: Also real. Free tiers on these tools commonly cap things like private project count or how long a program can run before timing out. None of that blocks a beginner course, but it's worth a two-minute check rather than a surprise later.

contentSections.synthesis: A browser-based editor is a genuinely real tool with a genuinely real limitation: it needs a connection, and free tiers have limits. Neither of those is a reason to avoid it — they're just facts worth knowing before you build a habit around it.

contentSections.body: For a long stretch of this track — likely the entire foundations phase — a browser-based editor is enough. There's no rush to install anything until you actually want the things installing gives you: working fully offline, a setup that feels fully "yours," or habits that carry straight into a future job, which is what lesson 2 covers.
A browser-based editor is a real tool with one real limitation: it needs a connection. That's a fair trade for zero setup.
