title: Installing an editor properly, when you're ready
description: What an installed editor like VS Code (free, works offline) gives you over a browser-based one, and why there's no rush to install it before a day with the capacity for a new task.

learningObjectives.text: Explain what installing a code editor adds beyond a browser-based one
Install a code editor by following the steps in the correct order
Recognise that installing is worth postponing to a higher-capacity day, not a test of readiness

contentSections.body: You've written a few lines in the browser editor and it worked fine. So why would anyone bother installing something? The honest answer: not for beginners' first week, but for a few real things that show up once you're coding regularly.

contentSections.question: Put the steps of installing VS Code — a free, widely used code editor made by Microsoft — into the order you'd actually follow them.
steps: Go to the official VS Code website and download the installer for your operating system
Run the installer and click through its prompts
Open VS Code for the first time
Create (or choose) a folder to hold your project's files
Open that folder from inside VS Code
contentSections.explanation: Nothing here is more mysterious than Module 1's top-to-bottom rule applied to a real-world task instead of code: each step needs the previous one finished. VS Code itself is free with no hidden cost to install — if the download or install fails for any reason, the browser-based editor from lesson 1 keeps working exactly the same in the meantime.

contentSections.body: An installed editor gives you three things a browser-based one mostly can't: it works fully offline (no connection needed once it's set up), it keeps your files as real files on your own device rather than on someone else's server, and it's the same tool most professional developers use day to day, so habits built here carry forward directly. None of that is urgent for someone just starting — it becomes useful once you're coding often enough that offline access and "my files, on my device" start to matter.
Installing buys offline access and files that live on your own device — genuinely useful, but not required to start.

contentSections.title: You don't have to install today

contentSections.body: There's a specific, avoidable way this goes wrong: attempting an install on the exact day it's hardest to troubleshoot anything.

contentSections.scenario: A learner installs VS Code during a bad flare — fog, low focus, a confusing installer screen they can't quite parse. They get stuck, give up, and decide coding "isn't for them."
contentSections.question: What's actually behind this outcome?

options.label: They lack the aptitude for this kind of work
They attempted a new, unfamiliar task during a stretch with the least capacity for it
VS Code's installer is unusually bad

feedback.aptitude: There's no evidence for this in the scenario — the difficulty shown up here is entirely explainable by timing, without needing to reach for a verdict on ability.
feedback.timing: Right. Reading an unfamiliar installer screen and troubleshooting anything odd about it takes exactly the kind of focus that's hardest to access during a flare. The same screen, on a better day, would likely be a two-minute non-event.
feedback.tool: VS Code's installer is fairly ordinary as these things go — nothing in the scenario points to it being unusually broken, just unfamiliar and encountered at a bad moment.

contentSections.mechanism: New, fiddly tasks are disproportionately hard during low capacity for anyone, regardless of skill — that's a timing problem, not a competence one. Since the browser-based editor from lesson 1 remains fully valid the whole time, installing has no deadline. It's worth doing on a day that actually has room for a new task, not the day it happens to occur to you.

contentSections.body: There's no test attached to installing software, and no clock running against it. The plan that survives variable capacity is the one where "install VS Code" sits on a list for a decent day, while the browser-based editor keeps the actual coding practice going in the meantime — so a stalled install never has to mean a stalled habit.
Install when a day has room for something new — not because a deadline says so, because none exists.

title: The terminal: five commands and no more for now
description: The terminal isn't a mystery box — it's a place you type exact words and it does exactly what they say. Five commands cover everything this track needs for now.

learningObjectives.text: Use five terminal commands (pwd, ls, cd, mkdir, node) to navigate and run code
Explain why the terminal requires exact spelling and no more
Recognise a "command not found" message as a typo, not a broken tool

contentSections.body: Someone's instructions say "just open a terminal and run this," and you're staring at a blinking cursor on a black rectangle with absolutely no idea what it wants from you. It wants exactly five things, for now, and nothing else.

contentSections.intro: Assemble your five-command terminal starter kit — the only commands this track needs for a while.

options: Shows which folder you're currently in
Deletes the current folder
Opens a text editor
fields.correctValue: Shows which folder you're currently in
fields.feedback: Right — pwd ("print working directory") answers "where am I right now," which is the very first thing worth checking when nothing seems to be where you expect.

options: Lists everything inside the current folder
Logs you out
Runs a program
fields.correctValue: Lists everything inside the current folder
fields.feedback: Right — ls shows you what's actually sitting in the folder you're in, which is how you confirm a file exists before trying to use it.

options: Copies a folder called project-name
Moves you into the folder called project-name
Creates a file called project-name
fields.correctValue: Moves you into the folder called project-name
fields.feedback: Right — cd ("change directory") moves you from where you are into a named folder, assuming that folder exists where you're currently standing.

options: Moves into project-name
Creates a new folder called project-name
Runs project-name as a program
fields.correctValue: Creates a new folder called project-name
fields.feedback: Right — mkdir ("make directory") creates a brand new, empty folder with that name, ready to cd into.

options: Opens app.js in a text editor
Runs app.js as a program and shows its output
Deletes app.js
fields.correctValue: Runs app.js as a program and shows its output
fields.feedback: Right — node runs a JavaScript file as an actual program, executing it top to bottom exactly the way Module 1 described, and shows whatever it prints.

contentSections.synthesis: Where am I (pwd), what's here (ls), go there (cd), make a new place (mkdir), run this (node app.js). That's the entire kit for now — enough to navigate to a project and run it.

contentSections.body: The terminal doesn't guess, doesn't autocorrect, and doesn't infer what you meant — it reads exactly what you typed and either recognizes it as a known command or doesn't. That's not the terminal being unfriendly; it's the same literal-instructions idea from Module 1, applied to a tool instead of a program. Get the exact spelling and spacing right, and these five commands will take you almost anywhere this track needs to go for a long while.
Five commands — pwd, ls, cd, mkdir, node — cover almost everything a beginner needs from a terminal.

contentSections.title: Typos are the terminal's whole personality

contentSections.body: You type a command, hit enter, and get back a red-looking line that says something like "command not found." It feels like an accusation. It's actually the most boring possible message: a typo.

contentSections.code:
$ sd my-project
command not found: sd
contentSections.question: The learner meant to move into their project folder. What actually went wrong?

options.label: The folder my-project doesn't exist
"sd" isn't a real command — it's a typo of "cd"
The terminal needs to be restarted

feedback.folder: The terminal never even got as far as checking whether my-project exists — it stopped at the very first word, because "sd" itself isn't a command it recognizes.
feedback.typo: Right. "sd" and "cd" differ by one letter, and the terminal treats them as two completely unrelated words — one it knows, one it's never heard of. This is the single most common beginner terminal error, and it's always this boring.
feedback.restart: Nothing here suggests the terminal is malfunctioning — it's responding exactly as designed to a command it genuinely doesn't recognize.

contentSections.flawExplanation: "Command not found" means precisely what it says: the first word you typed isn't in the terminal's list of known commands. It says nothing about your folders, your files, or whether the terminal is working correctly — it is working correctly, reporting an unrecognized word. The fix is almost always to reread exactly what you typed against what you meant to type, letter by letter.

contentSections.body: This is worth internalizing early, because it removes a lot of unnecessary alarm: a terminal error is not a verdict on you, and it's rarely a sign anything is actually broken. It's the terminal doing the one thing it's built to do — refuse to guess — and telling you plainly which exact word it didn't recognize. Module 4 goes much deeper into reading error messages like this one; this is the gentlest possible preview.
"Command not found" almost always means: reread exactly what you typed, letter by letter.

title: Files, folders and where your code actually lives
description: Why the terminal, the editor and the file system all need to agree on where a file actually is — and how one project folder with sane names prevents most of the confusion.

learningObjectives.text: Explain why a terminal command can fail to find a file the editor shows as open
Diagnose a file-not-found situation by checking the terminal's current folder
Organise a project into one folder with clear, consistent file names

contentSections.title: Your project needs one home, not scattered pieces

contentSections.body: You save a file, come back to run it, and the terminal insists it doesn't exist — while it's sitting right there, open, in your editor. Nothing is broken. Two tools are just looking in different places.

contentSections.scenario: A learner's editor has app.js open and saved. In the terminal, `node app.js` responds: "Cannot find module 'app.js'". They double- and triple-check the file is really there — it is.
contentSections.question: What's actually causing this?

options.label: The file itself is broken somehow
The terminal's current folder isn't where the file was actually saved
node.js can't run files created in a browser-based or installed editor

feedback.broken: The file being open and visible in the editor is good evidence it's completely intact — nothing about "cannot find module" points at file corruption.
feedback.location: Right. The terminal only ever looks inside the one folder it currently considers "here" — a location that has nothing to do with which file is open in a separate application like the editor.
feedback.toolmismatch: There's no such incompatibility — node.js runs any valid JavaScript file regardless of which editor created it. This isn't a tool-compatibility issue.

contentSections.mechanism: The terminal and the editor are two separate programs, each with their own idea of "where things are." The editor shows you a file because it opened it directly by path. The terminal only sees whatever's inside its own current folder — which you can always check with `pwd`, then confirm with `ls`. When the two disagree, the file usually exists; it's just not where the terminal is currently standing.

contentSections.body: This single mismatch — "the terminal is somewhere else" — probably explains more early confusion than any actual bug does. The fix is a two-command habit: run `pwd` to see where the terminal thinks it is, then `ls` to see what it can actually find there. If the file you expect isn't in that list, `cd` into the right folder (or move the file) before trying again.
When the terminal can't find a file that clearly exists, check where the terminal thinks it is, not whether the file is broken.

contentSections.title: Naming things so future-you can find them

contentSections.body: final2.js, final2-ACTUAL.js, final2-use-this-one.js. Every one of those file names is a small, honest record of a moment someone meant to come back and clean it up later.

contentSections.scenario: You're setting up how you'll organize files for the rest of this track.
contentSections.question: Which of these habits genuinely help future-you find things later?

items.label: One project = one folder, with everything for it inside that folder
Descriptive, consistent names like grocery-list-app instead of project1
Saving new attempts by renaming the file (final, final2, final2-ACTUAL)
Letting files land wherever the save dialog defaults to — Downloads, Desktop, wherever

explanation.onefolder: This is the single highest-value habit here — everything about a project stays discoverable in one place, which is exactly what the terminal needs too (one folder to `cd` into).
explanation.descriptive: A name that describes what the thing actually is beats a name that just marks it as "the first one" — six months from now, project1 tells you nothing.
explanation.renaming: This is the classic version-chaos pattern. It feels like progress in the moment and produces exactly the file graveyard from the hook — multiple candidates, no clear current one.
explanation.scattered: Default save locations scatter a single project across several folders with no organizing thread, which is precisely the situation lesson 1's diagnosis exercise showed going wrong.

contentSections.synthesis: One folder per project, named for what it is, is nearly the whole system. It costs nothing extra to do from the start and prevents most of the confusion that shows up later.

contentSections.body: One project, one folder, one clear name. That single habit prevents most of the "where did that file go" moments.

title: Setting up for low light, low energy and one hand
description: Editor settings that address real physical barriers — light sensitivity, low energy for typing, one working hand — decided in advance rather than improvised on a hard day.

learningObjectives.text: Adjust editor settings (theme, font size) to address real physical barriers
Distinguish an accessibility setting from a cosmetic preference
Build a personal bad-day setup decided in advance

contentSections.title: The setup that survives a bad day

contentSections.body: Room's dark, one hand is barely cooperating, and the default editor is a wall of bright white with text sized for someone sitting upright at a desk in good light. None of that is fixed — it's just what loads before you change anything.

contentSections.scenario: A default code editor: white background, standard-size text, keyboard shortcuts that assume two working hands. You're using it lying down, in low light, on a day one hand isn't fully cooperating.
contentSections.question: What's actually adjustable here, versus what you'd just have to push through?

options.label: None of it — editors come as they are
Theme, font size, and how much you rely on typing shortcuts are all adjustable settings
Only the theme — font size and typing method are fixed

feedback.none: Almost everything about how an editor looks and how much typing it demands is a setting, not a fixed property of the tool.
feedback.adjustable: Right. Dark theme, larger font, and reducing how much shortcut-based typing you rely on (in favor of autocomplete, snippets, or voice input) are all things you set once and keep.
feedback.themeonly: Theme is the most visible one, but it's not alone — text size and how much of the interaction depends on precise multi-key shortcuts are just as adjustable.

contentSections.concept: Almost every editor barrier a beginner hits on a hard day is a default, not a limitation — and defaults exist to be changed. Dark mode addresses light sensitivity and eye strain. Larger font addresses focus and visual fatigue. Leaning on autocomplete and snippets instead of typing everything by hand addresses a day when hands aren't fully cooperating. None of these are "cheating" — they're the setup actually adjusting to the person using it, instead of the reverse.

contentSections.body: It's worth being specific about the difference between an accessibility setting and a cosmetic one, because they get lumped together and they're not the same thing. A cosmetic choice affects how something looks. An accessibility choice affects whether a session is usable at all — a bright white screen isn't just less pretty in low light, for a lot of people it's actively painful, which is a completely different category of problem than taste.
A dark theme and a bigger font aren't cosmetic extras — for a lot of bodies, they're what makes the session possible at all.
The best time to decide your dark-room, one-hand, low-energy setup is on a day you have the focus to decide it — exactly like lesson 5 of Module 1 said about a minimum viable coding session.

contentSections.intro: Assemble the setup you'll actually reach for on a genuinely bad day.

fields.prompt: Theme for low light or light sensitivity?
options: Whatever the default happens to be
A dark theme, set once and left on
fields.correctValue: A dark theme, set once and left on
fields.feedback: Setting it once, rather than deciding fresh each session, means it's already there on the exact day you'd have the least energy to go find the setting.

fields.prompt: Which device do you actually reach for on a low-energy day?
options: Whichever device you name in advance — phone, tablet, or laptop, propped however works
Decide in the moment
fields.correctValue: Whichever device you name in advance — phone, tablet, or laptop, propped however works
fields.feedback: Naming the actual device in advance (not "something small") removes a decision from a moment when decisions are hardest.

fields.prompt: What's your plan for a day typing is genuinely hard?
options: Push through normal typing regardless
A named alternative — voice-to-text, heavy autocomplete, or shorter sessions with more breaks
fields.correctValue: A named alternative — voice-to-text, heavy autocomplete, or shorter sessions with more breaks
fields.feedback: "Push through" isn't a plan, it's the absence of one. A named alternative means a hard-typing day still has a real option on the table.

contentSections.synthesis: Dark theme set once, a named device, and a real plan for hard-typing days — decided now, so a bad day doesn't have to invent a setup from nothing, the same principle Module 1 covered for the coding session itself.

contentSections.body: This whole lesson feeds directly into the module's lab: the setup you build there is meant to already have these choices baked in, so "starting to code" on a rough day is just opening something that's already configured for you, not a fresh negotiation with a bright, two-handed default every time.
Decide your bad-day setup on a good day. That's the whole trick.

title: Practice — Complete Seven Setup Tasks
description: Seven drills on the module's skills — terminal commands, file organization, and telling a real accessibility setting from a cosmetic one. No new concepts.

learningObjectives.text: Apply the module's setup skills — terminal commands, file location, accessible defaults — without new instruction

contentSections.body: Nothing new here — just the muscle of actually using what the five lessons covered, fast, in whatever order they come up.
pwd, ls, cd, mkdir, node — and a folder future-you can actually navigate. That's the whole setup skill.

title: Lab — Build the Setup You'll Use for the Rest of the Track
description: Choose your real environment, configure it around your actual body and devices, and write the cold-start note that lets you begin a session in under a minute, even foggy.

learningObjectives.text: Choose a primary and backup coding environment based on real constraints
Configure an editor for low light, low energy and variable typing ability
Write a documented cold-start procedure that starts a session in under a minute

contentSections.body: By the end of this lab you won't just have opinions about setups — you'll have one, built, tested, and written down clearly enough that a foggy version of you next week can follow it without having to think.

contentSections.title: Your cold-start setup
contentSections.brief: You're about to spend the next 90-plus hours of this track opening some coding environment, over and over, on days with wildly different amounts of energy. This lab makes that decision once, properly, instead of re-deciding it every session.
contentSections.deliverable: A working environment, documented, that you can start in under a minute.

stages.title: Choose your primary and backup
stages.instructions: Decide: browser-based editor, installed editor, or both? Name your primary (the one you'll reach for most sessions) and your backup (what you switch to if the primary is unavailable — no internet, editor won't open, whatever). Write one sentence justifying each choice against your actual situation, not a generic "best practice."
stages.checkpoint: You've named a specific primary and a specific backup, each with a one-sentence reason tied to your real circumstances.

stages.title: Configure it for your body
stages.instructions: In your chosen editor, set: a theme (dark if light sensitivity or low-light use applies to you), a font size you can read comfortably without leaning in, and — if typing is sometimes hard — note which alternative you'd lean on (autocomplete, voice-to-text, shorter sessions). Actually change these settings; don't just plan to.
stages.checkpoint: The theme and font size are actually changed in your editor right now, and you have a named plan for hard-typing days.

stages.title: Write the cold-start note
stages.instructions: Write down, in plain numbered steps, exactly what you do to go from "nothing open" to "ready to type code" — which device, which link or app, which folder. Time yourself doing it once, from a closed browser or unopened app. If it takes more than about a minute, cut a step rather than adding instructions.
stages.checkpoint: You have a numbered cold-start procedure, and you've timed yourself following it in under roughly a minute.

rubric.criterion: A primary and backup environment are both named
rubric.meets: Specific tools are named (not "an editor"), each with a one-sentence reason tied to your real situation.

rubric.criterion: Settings are actually configured, not just planned
rubric.meets: Theme and font size are changed in the real editor, checkable by opening it.

rubric.criterion: A hard-typing-day plan exists
rubric.meets: Names a specific alternative (voice-to-text, heavy autocomplete, shorter sessions), not "I'll manage."

rubric.criterion: The cold-start note is a real, followable procedure
rubric.meets: Numbered steps specific enough that a foggy version of you could follow them without guessing.

rubric.criterion: It's actually fast
rubric.meets: Timed at roughly under a minute from closed to ready-to-type; steps were cut, not left in, if it ran long.

contentSections.body: A setup you have to rebuild every session is friction. A setup you wrote down once is a habit that survives a bad week.

title: Checkpoint — A Setup That Works From Bed
description: Ten questions: five from this module, five reaching back to What Code Actually Is. Ungraded, untimed.

learningObjectives.text: Retrieve setup fundamentals and last module's core distinctions without looking them up

contentSections.title: Checkpoint — A Setup That Works From Bed

questions.from: This module — A Setup That Works From Bed
questions.prompt: What does a browser-based editor need on your device to work?

options.label: A powerful processor and lots of storage
Just a browser and an internet connection
A pre-installed programming language

questions.explanation: It runs almost entirely on a remote server — your device just needs to display a page and send keystrokes over a connection.

questions.from: This module — A Setup That Works From Bed
questions.prompt: What does installing an editor like VS Code give you that a browser-based one mostly can't?

options.label: The ability to write real, working code
Offline access and files that live on your own device
Faster typing speed

questions.explanation: Both produce equally real, working code. Installing adds offline access and local files — genuinely useful, but not required to start.

questions.from: This module — A Setup That Works From Bed
questions.prompt: What does the terminal message "command not found" actually mean?

options.label: The terminal has crashed
The first word you typed isn't a command the terminal recognizes — almost always a typo
The file you're trying to run is missing

questions.explanation: It's the terminal reporting, accurately, an unrecognized word — nearly always solved by rereading exactly what was typed.

questions.from: This module — A Setup That Works From Bed
questions.prompt: A terminal says it can't find a file you can see open in your editor. What's the most likely cause?

options.label: The file is corrupted
The terminal's current folder isn't the same folder the file is actually saved in
The editor and terminal can never work with the same files

questions.explanation: The editor opens files directly by location; the terminal only sees inside its own current folder. `pwd` and `ls` reveal the mismatch.

questions.from: This module — A Setup That Works From Bed
questions.prompt: Why is switching to a dark theme for light sensitivity not just a cosmetic choice?

options.label: It changes whether the session is actually usable for that person, not just how it looks
It makes code run faster
It's required by every code editor's terms of service

questions.explanation: A cosmetic choice affects appearance only. An accessibility choice affects whether the session is usable at all — that's the real distinction.

questions.from: Previous module — What Code Actually Is
questions.prompt: From What Code Actually Is: what makes an instruction something a computer can act on?

options.label: It's polite and clearly worded
It's exact enough that nothing is left for judgment
It's written in a real programming language, regardless of vagueness

questions.explanation: Exactness is what matters — "if moisture reads below 30%" works because there's no gap left for judgment; "if it's dry" doesn't.

questions.from: Previous module — What Code Actually Is
questions.prompt: From What Code Actually Is: in what order does a program's lines actually run?

options.label: Whichever order is most efficient
Top to bottom, one line at a time, in the order written
All at once

questions.explanation: One line at a time, top to bottom — the entire mechanism behind how a program executes, with no lookahead and nothing simultaneous.

questions.from: Previous module — What Code Actually Is
questions.prompt: From What Code Actually Is: why doesn't watching a tutorial transfer well to writing code from a blank editor?

options.label: Tutorials are usually low quality
Watching trains recognizing the next step; writing requires generating it from nothing
It transfers fine given enough total hours

questions.explanation: Recognition and recall are different skills — a blank editor specifically tests recall, which only typing your own code practices.

questions.from: Previous module — What Code Actually Is
questions.prompt: From What Code Actually Is: what determines whether a coding habit survives a genuinely bad week?

options.label: How disciplined the learner is
Whether the plan has a real, smaller version built in for low-capacity days
Natural talent

questions.explanation: A fixed high-effort plan breaks the first time capacity drops. A plan with a defined minimum version bends instead.

questions.from: Previous module — What Code Actually Is
questions.prompt: From What Code Actually Is: why isn't restarting in a "better" language usually the right response to your first real error?

options.label: It's against the rules of this course
That category of error exists in every language, and restarting mostly costs the syntax fluency already built
Every language's errors are identical anyway

questions.explanation: Most early errors are logic-level, not language-specific. Restarting doesn't remove the error category — it just resets syntax progress.

contentSections.body: Anything that didn't come back will return in a later checkpoint. That's the design, not a failure.

title: Output: making the computer say something
description: console.log is the one instruction that turns a silently-running program into one you can actually see doing something — and how to shape what it shows.

learningObjectives.text: Identify which lines of code actually produce visible output and which don't
Use console.log to display text and variables together
Format output using multiple comma-separated values

contentSections.title: console.log is how your program talks back

contentSections.body: You type your very first real line of code and click Run. This is the moment Module 1 was building toward — the instant a program actually says something back to you instead of staying a set of ideas on a page.

contentSections.question: Which one actually makes "Hello" appear on screen when the program runs?

options.label: "Hello"; on its own
// Hello
console.log("Hello");

feedback.bare: This line is valid JavaScript, but nothing about it says "show this to the person watching" — it just exists and gets discarded.
feedback.comment: Anything after `//` is a comment, meant only for a human reading the file. The computer skips it entirely, as if it weren't there.
feedback.log: Right. console.log is specifically the instruction that means "display this." Without it, running code can be doing real work with nothing visible to show for it.

contentSections.concept: A program can run perfectly and produce zero visible output, because running and displaying are two separate things. console.log is the bridge between them — it's how you tell the computer "take this value and show it to the person watching," rather than just holding it silently inside the program.

contentSections.body: This is worth being precise about because it explains a common early confusion: a program that "does nothing" when run often isn't broken at all — it just never told the computer to display anything. Every one of your programs from here on will use console.log constantly, because it's the only way you get to see what your code actually did.
A program can run correctly and show you nothing. console.log is what makes it visible.
console.log("Hello") is the easy version. The moment you want to show a label and a value together — "Age: 34", not just 34 on its own — there's a small choice to make about how to combine them.

contentSections.problem: Print a friendly line that combines a label and a stored value: given `let age = 34;`, produce output that reads exactly: Age: 34

steps.label: Identify the pieces
steps.work: There are two pieces: the label text "Age:" and the value stored in `age`.
steps.why: Before combining anything, it helps to name exactly what's being combined — a label (fixed text) and a variable (a value that could change).

steps.label: Pick a combining method
steps.work: console.log can take multiple values separated by commas: `console.log("Age:", age);` It automatically inserts a space between each value it's given.
steps.why: Commas hand console.log two separate things to display, rather than forcing you to glue them into one piece of text yourself.

steps.label: Check the result matches exactly
steps.work: Running `console.log("Age:", age);` with age set to 34 prints: Age: 34 — matching the target exactly, including the automatic space.
steps.why: Matching the output exactly (not roughly) is the actual test — an extra or missing space is a real, common near-miss.

faded.problem: Now do the same for a name: given `let name = "Priya";`, produce output that reads exactly: Name: Priya

blanks.prompt: What's the label text piece, in quotes?
blanks.why: The label is the fixed text that never changes — everything that isn't the variable.
Variables are used without quotes — quoting it would print the literal word "name" instead of Priya's actual value.
Two comma-separated values, label first then variable, produces "Name: Priya" with the automatic space in between.

contentSections.procedure: Name the fixed text and the variable separately, then hand both to console.log separated by a comma. It handles spacing between them automatically — you only supply the pieces.

contentSections.body: There's a second way to do the same thing — joining pieces with `+` into one string, like `console.log("Age: " + age)`. Both work. The comma version is usually easier to read with several pieces; `+` gives you exact control over spacing (you supply it yourself, inside the quotes). Neither is "more correct" — this is the same syntax-versus-logic distinction Module 1 covered: two spellings of the same idea.
console.log with commas prints multiple pieces with automatic spacing — the simplest way to combine a label and a value.

title: Changing a program and predicting the change first
description: Committing to a prediction before running a changed program, and changing one thing at a time so a surprise always points at exactly one cause.

learningObjectives.text: Predict the output of a small, specific change to a working program
Change one thing at a time so results are attributable to a single cause

contentSections.body: You're about to change one line of a working program. Before you run it, there's a habit worth building right now, in your very first programs, because it gets harder to start later: guess what will happen, out loud or on paper, before you find out.

contentSections.question: A program has `let count = 3; console.log(count);` and prints 3. You change the first line to `let count = 3 * 2;`. What will print now, and why is committing to that answer before running it actually useful?
contentSections.hint: The value stored is whatever the calculation produces, not the text of the calculation itself.
contentSections.answer: It prints 6 — `3 * 2` is calculated before being stored, so `count` simply holds 6 by the time it's printed. The reason committing to a prediction matters isn't the prediction itself; it's that a wrong prediction tells you exactly where your mental model of the program is off, while running code you haven't predicted teaches you almost nothing even when it works.

contentSections.body: This is the same guess-first idea you've been doing throughout this course, turned into a personal habit rather than something a lesson does to you. Before running a change: say out loud (or type in a note) what you expect. If you're right, you've confirmed your model of the program matches reality. If you're wrong, you've just found the exact gap between what you think the code does and what it actually does — which is far more useful than a silent surprise.
Predicting before running turns every change into a test of your understanding, not just a roll of the dice.

contentSections.title: Small changes, checked one at a time

contentSections.body: You change three things about a program at once — a variable name, a value, and a line order — run it, and something's wrong. Which of the three caused it? There's no way to tell, and that's the actual cost of batching changes.

contentSections.question: Put these into the order that keeps a change attributable to exactly one cause.
steps: Confirm the current program works, and note its current output
Make exactly one small change
Run it and compare the result to your prediction
If it matches, move on; if it doesn't, that one change is the only possible cause
contentSections.explanation: This sequence only works because of the "exactly one" step in the middle. Skip that, change several things at once, and a surprising result at the end has multiple possible causes instead of one — which is a much harder problem to untangle, and entirely avoidable.

contentSections.body: This habit will matter far more once Module 4 covers reading error messages, because the first question in debugging anything is almost always "what did I just change?" — and that question only has a clean answer if you changed one thing at a time. It costs a little patience now; it saves a lot of confusion later.
One change, then run, then check. A surprise should only ever have one possible cause.

title: Comments, and writing them for the you of next week
description: A comment earns its place by explaining why, not what — and the version of you reading this code in three weeks is the actual audience.

learningObjectives.text: Distinguish a comment that adds real information from one that just restates the code
Write a comment explaining why a line exists, not what it does

contentSections.body: You return to code you wrote weeks ago and find a comment above a strange-looking line: `// don't remove, breaks things`. It's true, and it tells you absolutely nothing about why. Whatever context made that comment feel sufficient at the time is long gone.

contentSections.question: What's the actual problem with this comment?

options.label: It's factually incorrect about what the code does
It restates the line in plainer words and adds nothing the code didn't already say
It should be written above the line instead of below it

feedback.wrong: The comment is entirely accurate — `age + 1` does add 1 to age. Accuracy isn't the problem here.
feedback.redundant: Right. Anyone who can read `age = age + 1;` already knows it adds 1 to age — the comment translates code into English without adding a single new fact.
feedback.position: It's already positioned correctly, directly above the line it describes — placement isn't the issue.

contentSections.flawExplanation: A comment worth its place answers a question the code itself can't answer on its own — *why* this is happening here, what breaks if it's removed, what non-obvious constraint it's working around. "What this line does" is the code's job, not the comment's. A useful version of this same comment might be: `// birthdays add a year, but only after the party — hence the +1 happens here, not on creation`, which explains something the arithmetic alone genuinely doesn't show.

contentSections.body: This distinction matters because comments cost real attention to write and to read — a file full of comments that just restate each line adds noise without adding understanding, and it trains you to skim past comments entirely, including the rare one that actually mattered. The habit worth building from your very first programs: before writing a comment, ask whether it says anything the code doesn't already say by itself.
A comment earns its place by saying why, not what. The code already says what.

The version of you reading this code again has less memory of today than you're imagining right now — foggier, further from the original problem, maybe under time pressure. A good comment is a note left specifically for that person.

contentSections.scenario: You're deciding which of these comments to actually keep in a small program you're writing.
contentSections.question: Which of these are genuinely useful to future-you?

items.label: "using +1 here, not +1000ms — the API returns whole seconds, not milliseconds"
"this looks redundant but the API sometimes returns the date twice — don't remove"
"set name variable" above let name = 'Alex';
"increment the counter" above counter = counter + 1;

explanation.unit: This saves future-you from a real, specific mistake — mixing up seconds and milliseconds is exactly the kind of thing that's invisible from the code alone and costly to get wrong.
explanation.dontdelete: This one actively prevents a bug: without it, a reasonable-looking cleanup ("this looks redundant, let me remove it") would break something the comment already explained.
explanation.setname: This is a caption, not a note — `let name = "Alex"` already says exactly this, out loud, in code.
explanation.increment: Same issue — `counter = counter + 1` already communicates "increment the counter" perfectly clearly on its own.

contentSections.synthesis: The useful comments all explain something invisible in the code itself: a unit assumption, a reason something that looks safe to delete isn't. That's the whole test — would removing this comment lose real information, or just remove a redundant caption?

contentSections.body: This isn't a rule to follow anxiously on every line — most lines need zero comments, and that's fine. It's a habit for the handful of moments where something in your code would look wrong, redundant, or arbitrary to a reader with no memory of writing it, and a single sentence would save that future reader real confusion.
Write the comment for someone with no memory of today — including, most often, you.

title: Breaking a program on purpose to see what happens
description: Deliberately breaking a working program, safely, to learn what specific mistakes look like before they happen by accident.

learningObjectives.text: Explain the value of deliberately breaking a program in a safe, throwaway copy
Diagnose why a specific small change breaks a program
Keep an untouched working copy so experimentation stays low-stakes

contentSections.title: Poking at the edges on purpose

contentSections.body: You have a working program. Instead of leaving it alone, you copy it, and on the copy, you break it on purpose — remove a bracket, misspell a word, delete a line — just to watch what happens. This feels like the opposite of careful. It's actually one of the fastest ways to learn.

contentSections.scenario: A working line: `console.log("Total:", total);` You remove the closing parenthesis on purpose, on a copy: `console.log("Total:", total;` Running it produces an error before anything prints.
contentSections.question: What's actually happening here?

options.label: The value of total is now invalid
The punctuation the parser needs to understand where the instruction ends is now missing
console.log has stopped working correctly

feedback.value: `total` itself hasn't changed at all — the value stored in it is exactly the same as before. The problem is unrelated to what total holds.
feedback.syntax: Right. The engine needs matched opening and closing parentheses to know where a console.log instruction actually ends. With one missing, it can't tell where the instruction stops, and it can't proceed at all.
feedback.toolbroken: console.log itself is completely fine — nothing about this experiment touched how console.log works, only the punctuation surrounding this one call to it.

contentSections.mechanism: A missing bracket or parenthesis isn't a logic problem — it's a punctuation problem the engine can't work around, because matched brackets are how it knows where one instruction ends and the next begins. Deliberately causing this once, calmly, on a throwaway copy, means the shape of this exact error is already familiar the next time it shows up by accident.

contentSections.body: This is the actual value of breaking things on purpose: meeting a specific kind of mistake on your own terms, with nothing at stake, instead of meeting the identical mistake for the first time by accident, mid-task, on something you actually care about. A little deliberate collection of "I recognize this shape of problem" makes Module 4's deeper dive into error messages land as recognition rather than as a brand-new kind of dread.
Breaking something on purpose, calmly, is cheaper than meeting the same break by accident, under pressure.

contentSections.title: What you learn from a controlled break

contentSections.body: The entire safety of this exercise depends on one unglamorous habit: a working copy has to survive the experiment somewhere, or "controlled" stops being true.

contentSections.scenario: You're about to start deliberately breaking a working program to see what happens.
contentSections.question: Which of these keep the experiment genuinely low-stakes?

items.label: Keep an untouched working copy somewhere before changing anything
Break exactly one thing at a time, the same discipline from lesson 2
Note what you changed and what broke, even in one short line
Just start deleting things until something interesting happens, and worry about getting back later

explanation.keepcopy: This is what actually makes it "safe" — a way back always exists, so there's nothing to lose by breaking the copy.
explanation.onething: Same reasoning as lesson 2: break one thing at a time and you know exactly what caused the exact error you're now looking at.
explanation.writeitdown: Even a one-line note ("removed closing paren → got a syntax error about the console.log line") turns a fleeting moment into something you can actually recall later.
explanation.noplan: This is the version that isn't actually safe — without a working copy or any record, "later" can turn into genuinely lost work and real frustration, the opposite of a low-stakes exercise.

contentSections.synthesis: Deliberate breaking stays cheap and useful exactly as long as it's genuinely controlled: a saved working copy, one change at a time, and a quick note of what happened. Skip those and it's not an experiment anymore — it's just an accident with extra steps.

contentSections.body: Treat this like a real, repeatable practice rather than a one-time curiosity: a few minutes now and then, on a copy of something already working, trying one small deliberate break and reading whatever the computer says back. It costs almost nothing and it's quietly one of the highest-value habits in this whole track.
Break it on a copy, break one thing at a time, and note what happened. That's what makes it a real experiment instead of an accident.

title: Typing less: snippets, autocomplete and copy-paste discipline
description: Letting the editor handle repetitive typing is a real accessibility win, not a shortcut for the lazy — with one non-negotiable rule for anything pasted in.

learningObjectives.text: Use autocomplete and snippets to reduce repetitive typing
Explain why reduced typing is an accessibility benefit, not a lesser way of coding
Read pasted code before running it, and explain why that matters more than for typed code

contentSections.title: Let the editor type the boring parts

contentSections.body: You're going to type `console.log(` more times this track than you'll ever count. On a day your hands are cooperating fully, that's a minor annoyance. On a day they aren't, it's a real cost — and it's one almost every editor already has a built-in answer for.

contentSections.question: You type `cons` and the editor offers to auto-complete it to `console.log()`, cursor already placed between the parentheses. For someone with limited hand stamina today, what's the actual value of accepting that suggestion, beyond just "it's quicker"?
contentSections.hint: Compare what changes about the finished code versus what changes about the physical effort of getting there.
contentSections.answer: Nothing about the resulting code is different — typed in full or completed from four letters and a tab, `console.log()` on the page is identical either way. What changes is the physical typing required to get there, which for anyone whose hands don't fully cooperate on a given day is a real, concrete accessibility difference, not a shortcut that produces "lesser" code.

contentSections.body: Autocomplete and snippets exist in essentially every code editor, browser-based or installed, and they're worth turning on and getting comfortable with from your very first programs — not once you're "advanced enough" to deserve them. Snippets specifically are pre-built templates (type a short trigger, get a whole common pattern inserted) for things you'll write repeatedly, like a console.log or a basic loop structure.
Typing less isn't cutting corners. It's the editor doing the boring, repetitive part so your effort goes where it matters.

You paste a chunk of code from a tutorial straight into your project, run it, and a variable you never touched has changed value. Nothing about pasting itself was wrong — reading it first is the step that got skipped.

contentSections.scenario: A learner copies a snippet from a tutorial and pastes it into their project without reading it first. It includes a line reassigning a variable with the same name as one they'd already set up earlier in their file. Running it, their earlier value is silently gone.
contentSections.question: What actually let this happen?

options.label: Copy-pasting code is inherently unsafe and should be avoided entirely
The pasted code was never read before it ran, so the name collision went unnoticed
The tutorial's code was written maliciously

feedback.avoid: Copy-pasting itself isn't the problem — plenty of legitimate code gets reused this way constantly, including by professionals. The gap here is specifically that it went straight from clipboard to running without a read.
feedback.unread: Right. Typing code yourself, even slowly copying it by hand, forces your eyes across every line at least once. Pasting skips that entirely — nothing forces a look before it runs.
feedback.malicious: Nothing in the scenario suggests bad intent — an accidental name collision between two ordinary variables is a completely mundane, common thing to happen, no ill will required.

contentSections.mechanism: Reading code before running it is what catches exactly this class of problem — a name already in use, a line that does more than the snippet's description suggested, an assumption about your project that doesn't actually hold. This matters specifically more for pasted code because typing, even slowly, is itself a forcing function for attention that pasting quietly removes.

contentSections.body: This isn't a rule against using other people's code, tutorials, or — as Module 5 covers directly — AI-generated code. It's the one habit that makes using any of those genuinely safe: read what's about to run in your own project before it runs, every time, no exceptions for how trustworthy the source seems.
Copy freely. Read before you run — every single time, regardless of the source.

title: Practice — Modify Eight Programs to Produce a Stated Output
description: Eight drills: given a working program and a target output, find the smallest correct change. No new concepts.

learningObjectives.text: Modify a small program to produce a specified output, changing only what's necessary

contentSections.body: Each of these gives you a working program and a target. The skill is finding the smallest change that gets there — not any change that happens to work, the smallest one that keeps everything else intact.
The smallest change that gets you to the target is almost always the right one.

title: Lab — Write a Program That Introduces You
description: Write, run, and polish a small program that prints a formatted introduction — your first real, finished, running program.

learningObjectives.text: Write a program using variables and console.log that produces formatted output
Add a comment that explains a genuine choice, not a restatement of the code
Self-check a finished program against an explicit rubric before calling it done

contentSections.body: Everything in this module has been building toward one small, real thing: a program that runs, produces output, and is genuinely yours — not a copied example with your name swapped in.

contentSections.title: A program that introduces you
contentSections.brief: Write a program that, when run, prints a short introduction — your choice of what to include: your name, something you're learning, a fact about you, whatever feels right. It should read like a real introduction, formatted deliberately, not a bare list of variable dumps.
contentSections.deliverable: A running program that prints a formatted introduction you wrote yourself.

stages.title: Decide what to say
stages.instructions: Before writing any code, write down (in plain English) exactly what you want your introduction to say — the actual sentences. Pick 3-5 pieces of information: your name and at least two others you choose. This stage produces no code at all yet.
stages.checkpoint: You have plain-English sentences for your introduction, with 3-5 specific pieces of information named.

stages.title: Turn it into variables and output
stages.instructions: Create a variable for each piece of information from stage one, then use console.log (with commas or + — your choice, per lesson 1) to print them combined into readable sentences. Run it. Compare the actual output to what you wrote in stage one, and adjust until they match.
stages.checkpoint: The program runs without errors and its printed output matches the introduction you planned in stage one.

stages.title: Add one real comment and self-check
stages.instructions: Add exactly one comment somewhere in the program that explains a genuine choice you made (why you picked a particular format, phrasing, or piece of information) — not a restatement of a line. Then run through the rubric below against your own program before calling it done.
stages.checkpoint: There's exactly one comment, and it explains a why rather than a what. You've checked your program against every rubric criterion.

rubric.criterion: The program runs without errors
rubric.meets: Running it produces output with no error message — you've actually run it, not just written it.

rubric.criterion: Output matches a real, planned introduction
rubric.meets: What prints matches the plain-English sentences from stage one, not an improvised version.

rubric.criterion: At least three pieces of information are shown
rubric.meets: Name plus at least two more, each stored in its own variable rather than hardcoded directly into console.log.

rubric.criterion: Output is formatted, not a raw variable dump
rubric.meets: Reads like a sentence a person would say, with labels or phrasing around the values, not just bare values printed one after another.

rubric.criterion: The one comment explains why, not what
rubric.meets: Removing the comment would lose real information about a choice you made — it doesn't just restate the line beneath it.

contentSections.body: This is your first finished, running, genuinely yours program. Everything after this module builds on the exact same moves: variables, output, one careful change at a time.

title: Checkpoint — Your First Programs

title: The error message is talking to you, in order
description: An error message has three plain parts — category, description, location — and none of them are commentary on you as a person.

learningObjectives.text: Identify the type, description and location within an error message
Explain that an error message is generated, neutral text, not a personal judgment

contentSections.body: You run your program and a wall of red text appears — words you don't recognize, a file path, some numbers. On a foggy day especially, the instinct is to close the tab. There's a real shortcut through this: every error message has the same three parts, in the same order, every time.

contentSections.scenario:
A real error message:

```
ReferenceError: total is not defined
    at Object.<anonymous> (/home/you/app.js:3:13)
```
contentSections.question: Which part tells you exactly where to look — which file, which line?

options.label: ReferenceError
total is not defined
/home/you/app.js:3:13

feedback.type: This names the category of problem — a reference to something that doesn't exist — which is useful context, but it doesn't say where.
feedback.desc: This describes the specific problem in plain terms, which helps you understand what happened — but still doesn't tell you which line to open.
feedback.location: Right. The file path, line number, and column number are the location — the exact spot to go look, out of everything in your project.

contentSections.concept: Every JavaScript error message has three parts, always in the same order: a **type** (the category — ReferenceError, TypeError, SyntaxError), a **description** (what specifically happened, in plain-ish words), and a **location** (which file, which line, sometimes which character). Learning to separate these three, on sight, turns a wall of red text into three short, specific facts.

contentSections.body: This structure holds regardless of which of these three parts feels most alarming at a glance. Once you can pull them apart, the process is almost mechanical: the location tells you where to go; the type gives you a category to think in; the description narrows it further. None of that requires understanding the whole error instantly — it just requires knowing which piece to read for which purpose.
Every error message has a type, a description, and a location — three separate facts, not one wall of alarming text.

"ReferenceError: total is not defined" reads a little like an accusation. It isn't one — it's the same generated sentence that would appear for anyone, on any skill level, who triggered the exact same condition.

contentSections.question: Why does an error message often feel personal or alarming, even though it's completely generic, generated text?
contentSections.hint: Think about the wording itself — words like "Error" and phrases like "is not defined" — versus what actually produced it.
contentSections.answer: The wording is blunt by design (short, technical, no softening language), and it shows up at a moment you're already invested in something working — a combination that reads as more personal than it is. But the text itself is generated identically for anyone who triggers that exact condition; it has no idea who wrote the code, how experienced they are, or why the mistake happened. It's closer to a smoke detector going off than a verdict.

contentSections.body: This reframe is worth holding onto specifically because Module 1 already established that a computer has no judgment to apply to anything — no gap-filling, no intuition, no opinions. That same fact applies here: an error message can't be disappointed in you, because disappointment requires a kind of judgment the computer simply doesn't have. It's reporting one specific, mechanical condition, in the same words it would use for anyone.
An error message is a smoke detector, not a verdict. It has no opinion about you — only a fact to report.

title: Syntax errors: the computer literally can't read it
description: A syntax error means the file couldn't even be parsed — the engine never got as far as running anything, which is why nothing prints, not even the lines that were fine.

learningObjectives.text: Explain why a syntax error blocks an entire file rather than just the broken line
Identify common syntax mistakes — unmatched quotes and brackets

contentSections.body: You run a program with three console.log lines. Nothing prints — not even the first one, which had nothing wrong with it at all. That's the single biggest clue you're looking at a syntax error, not a logic mistake.

contentSections.scenario: A program has three console.log lines. Line 2 is missing a closing parenthesis. Running the file produces a SyntaxError, and nothing prints — not even line 1, which is completely correct on its own.
contentSections.question: Why does a broken line 2 stop line 1's perfectly fine output from appearing at all?

options.label: Line 1 must have a hidden problem too
The whole file has to be readable before any of it runs — a syntax error blocks everything, not just the broken line
console.log requires every line in the file to also be console.log

feedback.hidden: Nothing in the scenario suggests line 1 has any problem — it's fully correct, and that's exactly the point being tested here.
feedback.wholefile: Right. Before a single line can execute, the entire file has to be successfully understood as valid code. A syntax error means that understanding-step failed completely — execution never starts, for any line.
feedback.rule: There's no such rule — console.log lines coexist with all kinds of other code constantly. This isn't about what kind of lines are present.

contentSections.mechanism: There are two separate phases: first the engine reads the whole file and checks it's structurally valid code (parsing), then it runs it top to bottom (execution) — the process Module 1 covered. A syntax error is a parsing-phase failure. Since parsing happens for the entire file before execution begins at all, a broken line 2 prevents line 1 from ever getting the chance to run, even though line 1 itself is fine.

contentSections.body: This is genuinely useful as a diagnostic signal on its own: if literally nothing printed, including things that should have worked, suspect a syntax error somewhere in the file — a missing bracket, an unclosed quote, a stray character. If some things printed and then it broke partway through, that's a different category entirely, and lesson 3 covers it.
Nothing printed at all, including the fine parts? Suspect a syntax error — the file never got past being read.
A handful of syntax mistakes cause the vast majority of a beginner's first errors, and they're almost always punctuation, not logic: a bracket left open, a quote never closed.

contentSections.question: This produces a SyntaxError before anything runs. What's the actual issue?

options.label: message is misspelled somewhere
The opening quote before "Hello" has no matching close — it swallows the rest of the line
console.log can't handle text containing a comma

feedback.spelling: message is spelled consistently in both lines — spelling isn't the issue here.
feedback.quote: Right. There's one opening quote and none to close it, so the string never technically ends — everything after it gets pulled into an unterminated piece of text the engine can't make sense of.
feedback.comma: Commas inside a string are completely normal and cause no problem — plenty of real messages include them.

contentSections.flawExplanation: This is the unmatched-quote pattern in its most common form: one quote character opens a string, and the intended closing quote is either missing or misplaced (here, entirely absent). Most editors color-highlight matched quotes and brackets specifically so this becomes visible before you ever hit run — glancing at that highlighting is a genuinely fast habit worth building.

contentSections.body: The most common syntax slips, in rough order of frequency: an opening bracket, parenthesis, or brace with no matching close (or one closed too early); a quote mark that opens a string but never closes it, swallowing everything after it; and a missing comma between items in a list. None of these are about whether your logic is right — they're about whether the shape of the code is even valid to read, which is why they get caught before execution starts at all.
Unmatched brackets and quotes cause most syntax errors. Your editor's highlighting is trying to show you exactly this.

title: Runtime errors: it read it and then it went wrong
description: A runtime error means the file was readable and execution genuinely began — the program broke partway through, and how far it got before breaking is real diagnostic information.

learningObjectives.text: Distinguish a runtime error from a syntax error by how far the program got
Recognise common runtime error types and their likely causes

contentSections.title: It got further before it broke

contentSections.body: This time, some things actually printed before the error showed up. That single fact changes the whole diagnosis — this program was read successfully and started running. Something else went wrong, later, in a completely different way.

contentSections.scenario: A program has four console.log lines. Lines 1 and 2 print their output normally. Then a TypeError appears, and lines 3 and 4 never run at all.
contentSections.question: What does the fact that lines 1 and 2 printed tell you?

options.label: Nothing — it could still be a syntax error somewhere else in the file
The file parsed successfully and execution genuinely began — this is a runtime error, encountered partway through
The program actually succeeded, since most of it printed

feedback.nothing: It actually tells you a great deal — lesson 2 established that a syntax error blocks the entire file, with nothing printing at all. Two lines genuinely printing rules that out.
feedback.runtime: Right. Since a syntax error would have silenced everything, including lines 1 and 2, their successful output proves the engine read the whole file fine and started executing top to bottom, exactly as Module 1 described. The failure happened during that execution, not before it.
feedback.succeeded: Two out of four lines printing isn't success — lines 3 and 4 never ran at all, and whatever the program was meant to accomplish with them didn't happen.

contentSections.mechanism: A runtime error happens after parsing succeeds, once the engine is genuinely executing the program line by line and hits something it can't do — call something that isn't a function, read a property off a value that's empty, use a name correctly spelled but never actually assigned anything real. "How far did it get" (what already printed) is one of the fastest diagnostic questions available, because it instantly separates a parsing-phase problem from an execution-phase one.

contentSections.body: This distinction between syntax and runtime errors is worth having automatic, because it points you toward a completely different kind of fix. Nothing printed at all? Look for a punctuation problem — a bracket, a quote. Some things printed, then it broke? Look at the specific line where it stopped, and the specific value it was trying to work with at that moment.
What already printed before the error is real information. It tells you the file was readable and execution genuinely started.

contentSections.title: Common shapes of a runtime error

contentSections.body: Runtime errors come in a small number of recognizable shapes, and learning to recognize the shape — before untangling every detail — narrows down what you're even looking for.

contentSections.scenario: A variable is declared but never given a real value: `let data; console.log(data.trim());` — data currently holds `undefined`, and the line tries to call `.trim()` on it.
contentSections.question: Which error type does this situation produce?

options.label: ReferenceError
TypeError
SyntaxError

feedback.reference: `data` does exist as a name — it was declared with `let data;`. ReferenceError is specifically for names the engine has never encountered at all, which isn't the case here.
feedback.type: Right. `data` exists but currently holds `undefined`, and `undefined` has no `.trim()` method — trying to call it is asking a value to do something its actual type can't support, which is exactly what TypeError signals.
feedback.syntax: The file parses just fine — there's no punctuation problem here. This error only shows up once the line actually runs, which rules out a syntax error entirely.

contentSections.concept: TypeError doesn't mean a name is missing — it means the value that name currently holds can't do what you're asking of it. `undefined` is a value like any other; it's simply one with no methods of its own, which is why calling a method on it is one of the most common ways to trigger a TypeError.

contentSections.body: Two runtime error types cover an enormous share of a beginner's early mistakes. **ReferenceError** means a name was used that the engine has genuinely never encountered — a typo in a variable name, or a variable used before Module 1's top-to-bottom rule has reached the line that creates it. **TypeError** is broader: it covers trying to do something with a value that its actual type can't support right now — calling something as a function when it isn't one, or reaching for a property on a value that turned out to be undefined instead of the object you expected.
ReferenceError means a name doesn't exist. TypeError means you asked a value to do something its current type can't support.

title: The stack trace, from the bottom up
description: A stack trace with multiple lines isn't a wall of noise — it's a chain of function calls, and finding your own file among them is the fastest way in.

learningObjectives.text: Locate the frame in a stack trace that points to your own code
Reconstruct the chain of function calls a stack trace describes

contentSections.body: A stack trace with six or seven "at ..." lines looks like it wants a computer science degree to parse. It doesn't. It's just several function calls, listed in order, and you only need to find the one that's actually yours.

contentSections.problem: A stack trace shows several "at" lines — some referencing internal Node.js modules, one referencing your own file, app.js, at line 12. Find the line worth acting on first.

steps.label: Scan for your own filename
steps.work: Read down the list of "at ..." lines looking specifically for the one that names a file you actually wrote — here, app.js — rather than a library or internal module path.
steps.why: You can't edit code you didn't write, and generally shouldn't try to — the frames from libraries and internals explain the chain, but they're not where a fix belongs.

steps.label: Note the exact line number in that frame
steps.work: The app.js frame reads something like "at Object.<anonymous> (/home/you/app.js:12:5)" — line 12, character 5.
steps.why: This is the specific place in your own code that either caused the problem directly, or is where you called into whatever eventually caused it.

steps.label: Read the error's type and description first, then go to that line
steps.work: Combine what the error type and message already told you (lesson 1 and 3's skills) with this specific location to form a concrete guess about what's wrong at that exact line.
steps.why: The location alone doesn't explain the problem — pairing it with the type and description from earlier in the message is what turns a location into an actual diagnosis.

faded.problem: A different stack trace has frames for three internal library files and one for your file, utils.js, at line 7. Where do you look first?

blanks.prompt: Which filename are you scanning for among the frames?
blanks.why: It's the only frame representing code you actually wrote and can change — the others are context, not action items.

blanks.prompt: What line number does that frame point to?
blanks.why: The line number is the exact spot to open in that file — no need to read the whole thing, just that line and its immediate surroundings.

blanks.prompt: What do you read from the error message before going to that line?
blanks.why: Type and description (from lesson 1 and 3) tell you roughly what kind of problem to expect once you get to line 7 — going in with that context makes the line much faster to interpret.

contentSections.procedure: Scan the trace for the frame naming your own file, note its exact line, then combine that location with the error's type and description to form a concrete diagnosis — not one without the other.

contentSections.body: Library and internal frames aren't useless — they show the path the program took to get where it broke, which lesson 4's second pod covers directly. But when time and energy are limited, the frame naming your own file is almost always the highest-value place to look first, because it's the one place you can actually make a change.
Among several stack trace lines, find the one naming your own file first. That's where you can actually act.

contentSections.title: The chain of calls that got you there

contentSections.body: Your code calls a function, which calls another function, which calls another — and the error happens three layers deep. The stack trace's multiple lines are the record of exactly that chain.

contentSections.question: getGreeting() calls formatName(), which calls capitalize(), where the error actually happens. Reconstruct the order these calls occurred in, from your original code outward to the actual failure.
steps: Your top-level code calls getGreeting()
getGreeting() calls formatName()
formatName() calls capitalize()
capitalize() is where the error actually occurs
contentSections.explanation: This chain is exactly what a multi-line stack trace is recording: each function called the next, one level deeper, until the innermost one hit trouble. Reading from your own entry point toward the specific point of failure tells the whole story of how the program got there — not just where it ended up.

contentSections.body: You don't need to fully trace every intermediate frame to fix most beginner errors — the frame naming your own file is usually enough. But recognizing that a stack trace is a call chain, not a random pile of text, makes the ones you do need to read fully feel far more like a map and far less like noise.
A stack trace with several lines is a chain of calls, not a wall of noise — each line is one link in the story.

title: Searching an error message usefully
description: Stripping an error message down to the part that's genuinely searchable, and judging whether what you find is actually trustworthy before pasting it into your project.

learningObjectives.text: Write a search query from an error message that keeps the generalizable parts and drops the specific ones
Evaluate whether a search result is trustworthy before applying its fix

contentSections.title: What to keep, what to cut

contentSections.body: You paste your entire error message into a search bar — file path, project name, line numbers and all — and get back nothing useful. Nobody else's project has your exact file path. That's the whole problem.

contentSections.scenario:
Two candidate search queries for the same error:

**A:** `TypeError Cannot read properties of undefined reading toUpperCase /home/roi/my-grocery-app/index.js:14:23`

**B:** `TypeError Cannot read properties of undefined toUpperCase`
contentSections.question: Which query is more likely to find genuinely useful results?

options.label: Query A, with the full path and line numbers included
Query B, with the specifics stripped out
Neither — error messages generally aren't worth searching

feedback.a: The file path and line numbers here belong to one specific project on one specific machine — nobody else's search results will ever match that exact text.
feedback.b: Right. Stripped down to the error type and general description, this is the part that would be identical for anyone hitting the same underlying problem, which is exactly what makes it findable.
feedback.neither: Error messages are genuinely one of the most searchable things in programming — the trick is knowing which part of the message to actually search for.

contentSections.concept: An error message mixes two kinds of content: the general part (type and core description) shared by anyone hitting the same issue, and the specific part (your file path, project name, exact line) that belongs only to you. A useful query keeps the first and drops the second.

contentSections.body: This distinction holds regardless of which specific error you're looking at: the general part is the part worth typing into a search bar, and the specific part is the part worth leaving out entirely, no matter how prominently it appears in the original message.
Keep the error type and the general description. Drop your file path, project name, and line numbers — they're yours alone.

A search turns up five different answers to what looks like the same problem. Some are years old, some are for a different language entirely, one is confidently wrong. Finding results was the easy part.

contentSections.scenario: You've found several results for your error message and need to decide which, if any, to actually trust.
contentSections.question: Which of these are genuine signals a result is worth trusting?

items.label: It mentions your exact error type and a very similar description
It's reasonably recent, or at least not clearly outdated for your setup
It's written very confidently and sounds certain
It comes from official documentation or a well-established source, not an anonymous unverified post

explanation.exactmatch: This is the single strongest signal — a result addressing your specific error type and description is far more likely to be genuinely relevant than one that's merely adjacent.
explanation.recent: Software changes over time; a fix from years ago for an old version can be actively wrong for what you're using now.
explanation.confident: Confidence and correctness are unrelated — plenty of wrong answers online are written with total certainty. This is worth actively distrusting as a signal.
explanation.source: A source with some accountability behind it (official docs, an established, moderated site) is more likely to have been checked by someone else than an anonymous one-off post.

contentSections.synthesis: Match the exact error, check it isn't stale, and weigh the source — not how confident it sounds. And whatever you find still gets read before it runs, the exact same rule Module 3 already established for any pasted code, regardless of how trustworthy the source looked.

contentSections.body: This same judgment — matching precisely, checking for staleness, weighing the source, reading before running — is almost exactly the skill Module 5 builds on next, for getting and checking help from an AI tool instead of a search engine. The underlying discipline doesn't change: information from outside your own head still has to be checked against your actual situation before you trust it.
A confident answer isn't a correct one. Match the exact error, check the date, weigh the source — then still read it before you run it.

contentSections.body: This program introduces you (from Module 3's lab) five times, and gets it wrong five different ways. Every mistake here is deliberate, and every one of them is fixable using exactly the skills this module just covered.

contentSections.title: Debug a program with five faults
contentSections.brief: Start from a small introduction-style program (similar to Module 3's lab) with five separate, deliberate mistakes planted in it — a mix of syntax and runtime errors, exactly the kinds this module covered. Fix them one at a time, in the order the errors actually surface, not in the order you guess they might be.

stages.title: Run it and read the first error carefully
stages.instructions: Write your own version of a small introduction program (reuse or rebuild Module 3's lab program), then deliberately introduce five faults: at least one syntax error (a missing bracket or quote) and at least one runtime error (a misspelled variable, a value used before it's ready).
