stages.instructions: Fix only the current error, then rerun the whole program — don't fix multiple things at once, per Module 3's one-change-at-a-time discipline. For each error you encounter, note (in a line or two) whether it was a syntax error or a runtime error, and how you could tell. Continue until the program runs cleanly with correct output.
stages.checkpoint: The program now runs without any errors and produces correct introduction output, and you have a note for each of the five errors.

stages.title: Write the note and self-check

rubric.criterion: All five deliberate faults are actually fixed
rubric.meets: The program runs cleanly with no errors and produces the intended output.

rubric.criterion: Fixes were made one at a time
rubric.meets: Each error was addressed and rerun individually, not several changes made blind before running again.

rubric.criterion: Each note correctly identifies syntax vs. runtime
rubric.meets: For every error, the note states which category it was and cites the actual evidence (what did or didn't print) rather than a guess.

rubric.criterion: Each note explains what the message actually said
rubric.meets: Names the error's type, description, and location in your own words — not just "it was broken, now it's fixed."

rubric.criterion: The notes would help someone else facing the same five errors
rubric.meets: A stranger reading only your notes could recognize and fix the same category of mistake if they hit it.

title: What to include so the answer is about your problem
description: An AI tool can't guess what it isn't told — the actual code, the actual error, and what you expected are what turn a generic answer into one about your specific problem.

learningObjectives.text: Identify what a coding help request needs to be specific rather than generic
Write a request that includes actual code, actual errors, and expected versus actual results

contentSections.body: You type "my code doesn't work, please fix it" into an AI tool and get back a generic checklist that could apply to almost any program ever written. Nothing about your actual problem made it into the request, so nothing about your actual problem could make it into the answer.

contentSections.scenario:
Two ways to ask an AI tool for help with the same broken program.

**A:** "My code doesn't work, please fix it."

**B:** "This should print a total but I get `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'price')` — here's the code: [pasted code]. I expected it to print the total price."
contentSections.question: Which is more likely to get an answer about your specific problem?

options.label: A — shorter and to the point
B — includes the actual code, the actual error, and what was expected
Both equally — the AI can infer the missing details

feedback.a: "Doesn't work" could describe dozens of unrelated problems. Brevity here isn't precision, it's just an absence of information.
feedback.b: Right. Three concrete anchors — the real code, the exact error, and the expected result — leave almost nothing for the AI to guess at.
feedback.equal: An AI tool has no access to your screen, your intentions, or your project beyond what's in the message — it can't infer details that were never provided.

contentSections.concept: This is Module 1's core idea about instructions, applied directly to asking for help: a request with no gaps left for guessing gets a specific, useful answer; a vague one forces guessing on the other end, and a guess about a problem it can't actually see tends to land on generic advice rather than your actual fix.

contentSections.body: This matters more with an AI tool than it might with a human, oddly enough — a human colleague might ask a follow-up question before answering. Many AI interactions just answer the prompt as given, gaps and all, which means the burden of including enough information sits entirely with the request, not with a back-and-forth that fills gaps in later.
An AI tool can't see your screen or guess your intentions. What isn't in the request isn't in the answer.

contentSections.title: Building the request piece by piece

contentSections.body: A friend, also learning, keeps getting generic answers and can't figure out why. Their requests are polite, clear sentences — they just never include the one thing that would make the answer specific: the actual code.

contentSections.synthesis: Actual code, expected versus actual result, and the exact error message if there is one — that's the whole shape of a request specific enough to get a specific answer, no follow-up questions required.

contentSections.body: Real code, expected versus actual, exact error text. Three concrete anchors turn a generic request into a specific one.

title: Asking for an explanation, not just a fix
description: A fix changes your file for tonight. An explanation changes what you can do next time — and the difference comes down to what you actually ask for.

learningObjectives.text: Explain the practical difference between requesting a fix and requesting an explanation
Write a request that explicitly asks for the reasoning behind a fix

contentSections.title: The difference between a fix and an explanation

contentSections.body: You paste in a fix, it works, you move on. A week later the identical shape of bug shows up somewhere else, and it's as unfamiliar as the first time — nothing carried over, because nothing was ever asked to carry over.

contentSections.scenario: A learner asks an AI tool to "just fix this" for a bug involving an undefined value. It works. A week later, an almost identical bug appears in a different program, and they're completely stuck again.
contentSections.question: What's actually behind the lack of progress here?

options.label: The fix must have only been a temporary patch
The fix was applied without ever asking why it worked, so the underlying pattern was never learned
The two bugs are probably unrelated despite appearing similar

feedback.temporary: Nothing in the scenario suggests the fix stopped working — the actual gap is in what the learner understood, not in the durability of the code itself.
feedback.noexplanation: Right. "Just fix this" is a request for a fix, and that's exactly what it got — no reasoning was ever requested, so none was carried forward into the next similar situation.
feedback.unrelated: An "almost identical bug" in the scenario is, by its own description, closely related — the disconnect here is about what was learned, not about the bugs' relationship to each other.

contentSections.mechanism: A fix and an explanation answer two different questions. "Fix this" gets you working code for tonight. "Explain why this happens, then fix it" gets you working code plus a pattern you can recognize next time without needing to ask again. Neither request is wrong — but only one of them builds something that outlasts tonight's session.

contentSections.body: This isn't an argument against ever just wanting something fixed quickly — sometimes that's genuinely the right call, especially on a low-energy day. It's about noticing that the two requests get different things, so the choice between them is made on purpose rather than by default.
A fix changes your file for tonight. An explanation changes what you can do next time — and you have to ask for the second one specifically.

contentSections.title: A request that teaches you something

contentSections.body: Two requests can describe the identical bug in the same amount of detail and still get completely different value out of the answer, based on one extra sentence.

contentSections.scenario: You're deciding how to phrase a request so the answer teaches you something, not just fixes tonight's specific line.
contentSections.question: Which of these actually change what kind of answer you get?

items.label: Explicitly asking "explain why this happens" before or alongside asking for the fix
Asking what pattern to watch for so you'd catch it yourself next time
Being extra polite and using more formal language in the request
Making the request as long as possible, regardless of what it asks for

explanation.explainwhy: This directly requests the reasoning, which is the actual thing missing from a fix-only exchange.
explanation.pattern: This goes one step further — asking for the general shape of the mistake, not just this one instance of it, is what makes the learning transfer to a different bug later.
explanation.polite: Tone doesn't change what kind of information gets included in the answer — politeness and specificity are unrelated qualities of a request.
explanation.length: A long request that still only asks for corrected code will still just get corrected code — length alone doesn't add the missing "why" question.

contentSections.synthesis: What actually changes the answer is asking, plainly, for the reasoning and the pattern — not the tone or the length of the request around it.

contentSections.body: "Fix this" and "explain why this happens, then fix it" are two different requests. Only one of them teaches you anything.

title: Checking an answer you don't fully understand yet
description: There's real, useful checking available even before full understanding — running it, comparing output, reading the code line by line for anything that looks off.

learningObjectives.text: Identify which checks on an AI's answer are possible without full understanding
Apply a checklist to an AI-generated answer before trusting it

contentSections.title: Understanding enough to check, not enough to have written it

contentSections.body: An AI hands you five lines using a technique you've genuinely never seen. "I don't understand this yet" feels like it should mean "I can't check this at all." It doesn't — there's real, useful checking available before full understanding.

contentSections.scenario: You've been given a five-line AI fix using an unfamiliar technique. You don't understand every detail yet.
contentSections.question: Which of these can you still reasonably check right now, with the skills you already have?

options.label: Nothing at all, until you fully understand every line
Whether it runs without error, and whether the output matches what you expected
Only whether the explanation sounded confident

feedback.nothing: This treats understanding as all-or-nothing, but real checking doesn't require that — running code and comparing output are checks available right now.
feedback.runcheck: Right. Running it (Module 1's basic skill) and comparing the result to what you expected (Module 3's predict-first habit) are both genuinely useful checks that need zero mastery of the specific technique used.
feedback.confidence: Tone isn't a property of the code — it can't be verified, and it tells you nothing about whether the code is actually correct.

contentSections.concept: Full understanding and blind trust aren't the only two options. Between them sits a real, practical checking process: does it run, does the output match expectations, and — reading through even without full comprehension — does anything look obviously off. That's genuinely available at every stage of learning, including the very first week.

contentSections.body: This matters because waiting for full understanding before using anything would rule out most of what a beginner learns from in the first place — you learn the unfamiliar technique partly *by* using it and watching what it does, not only before touching it. The goal here isn't full comprehension on the first pass. It's a real, if partial, check that catches the most likely problems.
Full understanding and blind trust aren't the only two options. Running it and checking the output is real checking too.

contentSections.title: A checklist you can run before trusting it

contentSections.body: Turning "check it before trusting it" into an actual, repeatable list makes it something you reliably do, instead of something you mean to do and skip when you're tired.

contentSections.scenario: You're about to trust an AI-generated answer for a real problem in your own project.
contentSections.question: Which of these are genuinely useful checks to run first?

items.label: Read every line before running it, per Module 3's copy-paste rule
Actually run it and see what happens
Compare the actual output to what you expected, specifically
Trust it because it "sounds right" and matches the general shape of what you asked for

explanation.read: This is the same discipline Module 3 established for any pasted code, AI-generated or otherwise — read what's about to run in your project before it runs.
explanation.run: Actually running it is how you find out whether it works at all, rather than assuming from the description.
explanation.compare: This uses Module 3's predict-first habit directly — stating what you expected first makes a mismatch immediately visible instead of easy to miss.
explanation.soundsright: "Sounds right" is a feeling about the explanation's tone, not a fact about the code's correctness — this is exactly the trap lesson 4 covers next.

contentSections.synthesis: Read it, run it, compare the actual result to what you expected. None of that requires expert understanding — it requires actually looking, which is the whole checklist.

contentSections.body: This checklist is small enough to run every time, including on a low-energy day — it's a few minutes, not a deep audit. What it catches: an answer that doesn't actually run, one whose output doesn't match what you asked for, and — over time, as your reading skill grows from doing this repeatedly — logic that looks off even before you fully understand why.
Read it, run it, compare the output to what you expected. A small, repeatable checklist beats waiting for full understanding.

title: When the AI is confidently wrong, and how you'd know
description: Confidence in an AI's tone is generated the same way whether the answer is right or wrong — real signals worth double-checking are concrete, not about how sure it sounds.

learningObjectives.text: Explain why confident phrasing isn't evidence of correctness in an AI's answer
Recognise concrete signals that an AI answer is worth double-checking

contentSections.body: An AI tool tells you, with total confidence and no hedging, to call `array.total()`. It sounds exactly as sure of this as it would sound about something completely correct. That's the actual problem: the tone doesn't change.

contentSections.scenario: An AI confidently suggests `array.total()` to sum a list of numbers. Running it produces: `TypeError: array.total is not a function`.
contentSections.question: What's actually going on here?

options.label: The learner mistyped the function name while copying it
The AI generated a plausible-sounding function name that simply doesn't exist
array.total() exists but needs extra configuration

feedback.typo: Nothing in the scenario points to a copying mistake — the error is about the function itself not existing, not about a mismatched spelling.
feedback.hallucination: Right. The AI produced text that follows the pattern of a real answer — plausible name, confident delivery — without it corresponding to anything that actually exists.
feedback.config: There's no such function to configure — the error message says plainly that it isn't a function at all, not that it's missing some setup.

contentSections.mechanism: An AI tool generates text by predicting what a plausible answer looks like, based on patterns in what it's been trained on — it doesn't have a built-in, separate step that verifies a claim against a live, current source of truth before saying it confidently. Most of the time the patterns line up with reality closely enough that this doesn't matter. Sometimes they don't, and the result is a fluent, confident, wrong answer with no difference in tone to warn you.

contentSections.body: This is worth taking seriously without becoming a reason to distrust AI help generally — most answers are genuinely useful, and this module exists precisely because AI help is worth using well. The specific, actionable point is narrower: tone tells you nothing about correctness, so correctness has to come from somewhere else — the checking habits from lesson 3, applied here.
An AI sounds equally confident whether it's right or wrong. Tone isn't evidence — checking is.
Some situations are genuinely worth a second look before trusting an answer. None of them are about how the answer was phrased.

contentSections.scenario: You're deciding when an AI's answer is worth a second look before trusting it.
contentSections.question: Which of these are real, useful signals?

items.label: It confidently names something very specific you've never encountered before
It contradicts an error message you already read carefully
Two different AI answers to the same question genuinely disagree with each other
It's polished, uses complete sentences, and sounds sure of itself

explanation.unfamiliar: An unfamiliar, very specific claim (a function name, a library detail) is exactly the kind of thing worth verifying against a real reference before trusting.
explanation.contradicts: An error message is direct, observed evidence from your own system — an answer that contradicts it is contradicting something more concrete than the answer itself.
explanation.disagree: If two independent answers genuinely disagree, at least one of them has to be wrong — that disagreement alone is useful information.
explanation.polished: Polish is a property of writing quality, generated the same way regardless of accuracy. It's simply not connected to correctness.

contentSections.synthesis: The real signals are all concrete and checkable — an unfamiliar specific claim, a contradiction with observed evidence, disagreement between sources. Tone and polish aren't on that list at all.

contentSections.body: Double-check specific unfamiliar claims, contradictions with what you've observed, and disagreement between sources — not how confident something sounds.

title: Learning from the answer instead of pasting it
description: Pasting a working answer and moving on trains recognition, not recall — a small, deliberate habit of reproducing it yourself is what actually makes the learning stick.

learningObjectives.text: Explain why pasting an AI's answer trains recognition rather than recall
Build a personal habit for using AI help without losing the learning

contentSections.body: An AI hands you a working answer every single time you ask, all through this track and beyond it. Paste it in, move on, ask again next time — and somewhere in there, without a single dramatic moment, the actual learning can quietly stop happening.

contentSections.scenario: Two learners get identical working code from an AI for the same problem. One pastes it in and moves on immediately. The other reads it, closes the answer, and retypes the solution from memory, checking it against the original afterward.
contentSections.question: Which is more likely to solve a similar problem alone next week?

options.label: Both equally — same working code today either way
The one who retyped it from memory
The one who pasted it, since they covered more ground faster

feedback.equal: Today's working code is identical either way — the difference shows up next week, in a new problem neither of them has an answer pasted for yet.
feedback.retyped: Right. This is the exact recognition-versus-recall distinction Module 1 introduced for tutorials: reproducing something from memory, even right after seeing it, is a fundamentally different and stronger kind of practice than recognizing it as correct and pasting it.
feedback.pasted: Covering more problems today doesn't build the skill of solving one alone — it just accumulates more pasted answers, each equally unavailable next time.

contentSections.concept: Pasting a correct answer and moving on trains the same shallow skill watching a tutorial does: recognizing that something is right once it's shown to you. Producing it yourself — even having just seen the answer, even imperfectly — is recall, and recall is the actual skill a blank editor tests later, with nothing pasted to lean on.

contentSections.body: This isn't an argument against using AI help — it's genuinely one of the most useful tools available to a beginner, and this whole module exists to help you use it well. The distinction is about what happens in the moments right after a good answer arrives: whether it becomes something pasted and left behind, or something briefly practiced before moving on.
Pasting an answer trains recognizing it's right. Reproducing it yourself trains being able to do it again.

contentSections.title: A habit that keeps you actually learning

contentSections.body: The habit that keeps the learning alive doesn't have to be large — it has to be small enough to actually do every single time, including the tired ones.

contentSections.intro: Assemble your own personal rule for using AI help without losing the learning.
contentSections.objectName: your "use AI without losing the learning" habit

fields.prompt: Before pasting an AI's answer into your project, what do you do?
options: Paste it immediately and check later if there's time
Read it fully first, per Module 3's copy-paste rule
fields.correctValue: Read it fully first, per Module 3's copy-paste rule
fields.feedback: This is the exact rule Module 3 already established for any pasted code — read what's about to run before it runs, regardless of the source.

fields.prompt: After it works, what's the one small action that builds recall?
options: Move on to the next task immediately
Retype it from memory, or explain it back in your own words, before moving on
fields.correctValue: Retype it from memory, or explain it back in your own words, before moving on
fields.feedback: This is the small, repeatable action that turns "I saw this work" into "I can produce this myself" — the actual skill a future blank editor will test.

fields.prompt: What's worth capturing before you forget it?
options: Nothing — the code itself is the record
One sentence on what was actually new here, for your own future reference
fields.correctValue: One sentence on what was actually new here, for your own future reference
fields.feedback: A one-sentence note costs almost nothing and gives future-you (Module 1's recurring theme) something to search when a similar problem shows up again.

contentSections.synthesis: Read before pasting, retype or re-explain before moving on, note what was new in one sentence. Small enough to survive a tired night, real enough to actually build the skill.

contentSections.body: A small habit, done every time, beats a thorough one you only manage on good days. Pick the small one and actually keep it.

learningObjectives.text: Write a specific, well-formed request for AI coding help on a real problem
Check an AI's answer before trusting it, using a concrete checklist
Explain a solution's logic in your own words, without copying the AI's phrasing

contentSections.body: This is the whole module in one real pass: a genuine small problem, a request specific enough to get real help, a checked answer, and — the part that actually matters most — your own explanation of how it works, in your own words.

contentSections.title: Solve a problem with AI help, and explain it yourself
contentSections.brief: Pick a small, real coding problem — extend Module 3's introduction program, add a feature to Module 4's debugged program, or something new and small of your own choosing. Get AI help on it the well way: a specific request, a checked answer, and your own explanation afterward.

stages.title: Write a specific request

stages.title: Explain it in your own words, then self-check

rubric.meets: Included real code or a specific goal, an expected result, and an explicit request for reasoning, not just a fix.

rubric.criterion: The answer was actually checked

rubric.criterion: The explanation is in your own words

rubric.criterion: The explanation would actually help someone else
rubric.meets: A learner at the same starting point could follow your explanation and understand how the solution works.

contentSections.body: AI help, used well, is a specific request, a checked answer, and your own understanding at the end of it — not just a working file you don't quite understand.
